item.description: Full title: OpenFold3 on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: Predict biomolecular structures
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

OpenFold3 on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: Predict biomolecular structures

You can deploy OpenFold3-preview from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. The OpenFold Consortium and the AlQuraishi Lab at Columbia University developed OpenFold3 as an open source biomolecular structure prediction model. With a few lines of code, you can typically deploy OpenFold3 into your own AWS account. You can then predict the 3D structures of proteins, DNA, RNA, small-molecule ligands, and the complexes they form. The endpoint runs with network isolation, which you can use to help keep your sequences within your AWS account.

Computational drug discovery teams now use structure prediction as a core part of their work. Teams use it in target identification, antibody and protein engineering, and structure-based virtual screening. Teams have found running these models challenging. You need GPU infrastructure, a working CUDA and PyTorch stack, large model checkpoints, and a serving layer that handles requests that take minutes rather than milliseconds. SageMaker JumpStart can handle much of that work for you. OpenFold3 runs in an AWS-maintained container on a managed Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint. The endpoint is designed to handle request queuing and GPU warmup, and you can add autoscaling.

In this post, we show you how to:

  • Deploy OpenFold3-preview on a SageMaker asynchronous inference endpoint.
  • Submit structure prediction jobs and interpret the results, including predicted structures and confidence scores.
  • Run several predictions in parallel on multi-GPU instances.
  • Supply your own multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) to improve prediction accuracy while helping keep your sequences private.
  • Help reduce costs by scaling your endpoint to zero when it’s idle.

Overview of OpenFold3

OpenFold3 is an all-atom structure prediction model. It predicts the joint 3D structure of a set of molecules from their sequences. It isn’t limited to single protein chains: It can fold multi-chain protein complexes, protein–nucleic acid assemblies, and protein–ligand complexes in one prediction.

AttributeDetails
DeveloperOpenFold Consortium / AlQuraishi Lab, Columbia University
Model typeAll-atom biomolecular structure prediction
InputsProtein, DNA, and RNA sequences. Small-molecule ligands as SMILES
OutputsPredicted structures in mmCIF format, with confidence metrics (pLDDT, PAE, PDE)
VersionOpenFold3 0.4.1, of3-p2-155k checkpoint
LicenseApache 2.0
JumpStart model IDhuggingface-proteinfolding-openfold3
Supported instancesml.g6.2xlarge, ml.g6.4xlarge (default), ml.g6.12xlarge

The OpenFold3 developers release its code and model weights under the Apache 2.0 license, and they publish the training data and methods. Research organizations and pharmaceutical companies can inspect the model, fine-tune it, and build on it under the terms of that license. The developers describe OpenFold3-preview as a research preview.

Use cases

  • Target and complex structure prediction – Predict structures for targets that have no experimental structure, including multi-chain assemblies and protein–nucleic acid complexes.
  • Protein–ligand co-folding – Fold a protein together with a small molecule supplied as SMILES to generate binding-pose hypotheses for structure-based design.
  • Antibody and protein engineering – Evaluate designed variants by predicting their structures and comparing confidence across candidates.
  • High-throughput screening pipelines – Queue large batches of prediction jobs against an autoscaling endpoint and process the results directly from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).

Why OpenFold3 uses asynchronous inference

Most JumpStart models, such as large language models and embedding models, deploy to real-time endpoints. A real-time endpoint returns its response within a single request, and that request is capped at 60 seconds. Structure prediction works differently. Folding time grows with the number and length of the chains in a query, and real-world proteins and complexes often take several minutes.

For this reason, OpenFold3 on JumpStart runs on SageMaker Asynchronous Inference:

  • You upload the request to Amazon S3 and call InvokeEndpointAsync, which returns immediately.
  • The endpoint queues the request and processes it, with an invocation timeout of up to 1 hour.
  • The endpoint writes the result, or the error details, to an S3 location you choose. You can poll for it or get a notification through Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS).

Two properties of asynchronous endpoints suit scientific workloads especially well. First, they queue bursts of requests internally, so you can submit a large batch of sequences without building your own job queue. Second, they can scale to zero instances when the queue is empty, which helps you avoid paying for idle instances between experiments.

Prerequisites

To follow this walkthrough, you need:

  • An AWS account, and a SageMaker AI execution role for the endpoint. Following least privilege, this AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role needs read and write access only to the S3 prefix that you use for requests and results. For more information, see How to use SageMaker AI execution roles.
  • IAM permissions for the identity that runs the code: to create, describe, invoke, and delete the model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint, plus iam:PassRole for the execution role. For the optional scale-to-zero section, it also needs AWS Application Auto Scaling and Amazon CloudWatch alarm permissions. In production, scope these permissions to your resources rather than using broad managed policies such as AmazonSageMakerFullAccess. For more information, see Complete the prerequisites for asynchronous inference.
  • Access to Amazon SageMaker Studio, a SageMaker notebook instance, or a local IDE.
  • The SageMaker Python SDK v3 and py3Dmol, which you can install with pip install "sagemaker>=3,<4" py3Dmol.
  • Service quota for at least one ml.g6.4xlarge endpoint instance in your AWS Region. You also need quota for ml.g6.12xlarge if you follow the multi-GPU section. You can check your quotas and request increases in the Service Quotas console under Amazon SageMaker.
Important: SageMaker endpoints are billed per instance-hour while they’re running, including while they’re idle. To avoid unexpected charges, follow the Clean up section, or configure scale-to-zero as described later in this post. For pricing details, see Amazon SageMaker AI pricing.

Discover OpenFold3 in SageMaker JumpStart

  • Open SageMaker Studio and choose JumpStart in the navigation pane.
  • Search for OpenFold3.
  • Open the model card to review the model description, license, and supported instance types.
  • Open the example notebook from the model card. It contains the complete asynchronous deployment walkthrough shown in this post.

Deploy OpenFold3 with the SageMaker Python SDK

First, build the model from its JumpStart configuration and define an AsyncInferenceConfig. The output and failure paths are the S3 locations where the endpoint writes results and error details.

import json, time, uuid
import boto3
from sagemaker.core.helper.session_helper import Session
from sagemaker.core.inference_config import AsyncInferenceConfig
from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.configs import JumpStartConfig
from sagemaker.core.training.configs import Compute
from sagemaker.serve.model_builder import ModelBuilder

session = Session()
bucket = session.default_bucket()          # sagemaker-{region}-{account-id}
prefix = "openfold3-async"

model_builder = ModelBuilder.from_jumpstart_config(
    jumpstart_config=JumpStartConfig(
        model_id="huggingface-proteinfolding-openfold3",
        accept_eula=True,
    ),
    compute=Compute(instance_type="ml.g6.4xlarge"),
)
model = model_builder.build()

async_config = AsyncInferenceConfig(
    output_path=f"s3://{bucket}/{prefix}/output",
    failure_path=f"s3://{bucket}/{prefix}/failure",
)

endpoint = model_builder.deploy(inference_config=async_config)
endpoint_name = endpoint.endpoint_name
print(f"Deployed asynchronous endpoint: {endpoint_name}")

Setting accept_eula=True confirms that you’ve reviewed and accepted the model’s license terms, which is required to deploy this model. If you run this code outside SageMaker Studio, also pass your SageMaker execution role to ModelBuilder.from_jumpstart_config with role_arn="<role-arn>".

The endpoint stores your requests and results in Amazon S3, and they contain your sequences and predicted structures. For proprietary sequences, consider using a dedicated S3 bucket or prefix with server-side encryption using an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key that you manage. To encrypt results with your key, pass its ARN to AsyncInferenceConfig as kms_key_id. Restrict access with a bucket policy that allows only the roles that run this workflow, and add an S3 Lifecycle rule to expire request and result objects that you don’t need to keep. For more information, see Security best practices for Amazon S3.

Deployment typically completes within minutes. This includes a warmup step in which the container runs a short prediction on each GPU, so that the GPUs are warmed up when the endpoint reaches InService.

Tip: G6 capacity can be limited in some Regions. If a deployment fails with InsufficientInstanceCapacity, retry later, choose a different supported instance size, or deploy in another AWS Region where the model is available.

Run a structure prediction

A request is a JSON document with one or more named queries, and each query lists its chains. All chains in a query are folded together as one complex. Separate queries are folded independently.

Each chain has these fields:

  • molecule_type – protein, dna, rna, or ligand.
  • chain_ids – a list of chain identifiers, such as ["A"]. To specify identical copies, such as a homodimer, use ["A", "B"].
  • sequence – the residue sequence, for protein, DNA, and RNA chains.
  • smiles – a SMILES string, used for ligand chains instead of sequence.

The following example folds human ubiquitin, a well-characterized 76-residue protein:

s3 = boto3.client("s3")
smr = boto3.client("sagemaker-runtime")

payload = {
    "queries": {
        "ubiquitin": {
            "chains": [
                {
                    "molecule_type": "protein",
                    "chain_ids": ["A"],
                    "sequence": "MQIFVKTLTGKTITLEVEPSDTIENVKAKIQDKEGIPPDQQRLIFAGKQLEDGRTLSDYNIQKESTLHLVLRLRGG",
                }
            ]
        }
    }
}

# 1. Stage the request in S3
input_key = f"{prefix}/input/{uuid.uuid4().hex}.json"
s3.put_object(Bucket=bucket, Key=input_key, Body=json.dumps(payload).encode())

# 2. Submit asynchronously -- returns immediately
resp = smr.invoke_endpoint_async(
    EndpointName=endpoint_name,
    ContentType="application/json",
    InputLocation=f"s3://{bucket}/{input_key}",
    InvocationTimeoutSeconds=3600,
)
output_location, failure_location = resp["OutputLocation"], resp["FailureLocation"]

Then poll S3 for either the result or a failure record:

def split(uri):
    b, _, k = uri.removeprefix("s3://").partition("/")
    return b, k

result = None
for _ in range(120):                                    # up to ~30 minutes
    for loc, is_failure in ((output_location, False), (failure_location, True)):
        try:
            body = s3.get_object(Bucket=split(loc)[0], Key=split(loc)[1])["Body"].read()
        except s3.exceptions.NoSuchKey:
            continue
        if is_failure:
            raise RuntimeError(body.decode())
        result = json.loads(body)
    if result:
        break
    time.sleep(15)

if result is None:
    raise TimeoutError(f"No result yet; check {output_location}")
if result.get("status") == "error":
    raise RuntimeError(result["error"])

A request with invalid input, such as a malformed chain or an unsupported MSA name, still produces a result object, but with "status": "error" and an error message instead of structures. The last check surfaces that message.

Prediction time grows with the size of the input. In our tests on ml.g6.4xlarge, smaller proteins completed more quickly than larger proteins.

Interpret the results

The response contains a status, a list of predicted structures in mmCIF format, and their matching confidences. By default, OpenFold3 generates five diffusion samples per query, so each query returns five candidate structures. Each sample comes with two confidence files: a detailed one (_confidences.json) and a summary (_confidences_aggregated.json). The summary includes a sample_ranking_score that you can use to pick the best sample.

import os
os.makedirs("structures", exist_ok=True)
for s in result["structures"]:
    path = os.path.join("structures", os.path.basename(s["filename"]))
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        f.write(s["content"])
    print("saved", path, f'({s["size_bytes"]/1024:.0f} KB)')

summaries = {c["filename"]: c["data"] for c in result["confidences"]
             if c["filename"].endswith("_aggregated.json")}
for name, m in sorted(summaries.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]["sample_ranking_score"]):
    print(f'{name}: ranking={m["sample_ranking_score"]:.2f} pLDDT={m["avg_plddt"]:.1f} '
          f'pTM={m["ptm"]:.2f} ipTM={m["iptm"]:.2f}')

You can open the .cif files in any structure viewer, such as PyMOL, ChimeraX, or Mol*. To view a structure inline in a notebook, use py3Dmol:

import py3Dmol   # pip install py3Dmol
view = py3Dmol.view(width=600, height=450)
view.addModel(result["structures"][0]["content"], "cif")
# pLDDT is stored in the B-factor field: red = low confidence, blue = high
view.setStyle({"cartoon": {"colorscheme": {"prop": "b", "gradient": "roygb", "min": 50, "max": 90}}})
view.zoomTo(); view.show()

Figure 1: OpenFold3’s predicted structure of ubiquitin, rendered with the preceding code and colored by per-atom confidence (pLDDT). All figures in this post were rendered with 3Dmol.js (Rego and Koes, Bioinformatics, 2015).

The prediction shows ubiquitin’s compact fold: a mixed beta-sheet packed against a single alpha-helix. Most of the structure is blue (high confidence). Only the flexible C-terminal tail, at the top of the image, shifts toward yellow and red, which matches the tail’s known flexibility in experimental structures.

The confidence metrics tell you how much to trust each prediction:

  • pLDDT (predicted local distance difference test) – Per-atom confidence in the local structure, on a scale of 0–100. Higher is better, and values above about 70 generally indicate a reliable local structure. The summary file reports the average as avg_plddt.
  • pTM and ipTM (predicted TM-score and interface pTM) – Overall confidence in the fold, and in how chains and ligands are positioned relative to each other, on a scale of 0–1. For complexes, ipTM is the key number. The summary file also reports chain_pair_iptm for each pair of chains.
  • PAE (predicted aligned error) and PDE (predicted distance error) – Per-residue-pair error estimates, in the detailed confidence file. Use them to judge the relative placement of domains and chains.

Fold a complex

To predict a complex, list several chains in the same query. The following example co-folds human carbonic anhydrase II with its catalytic zinc ion and the drug acetazolamide. This is a well-studied complex with experimental structures in the Protein Data Bank (for example, PDB 3HS4):

ca2_sequence = (
    "MSHHWGYGKHNGPEHWHKDFPIAKGERQSPVDIDTHTAKYDPSLKPLSVSYDQATSLRILNNGHAFNVEFDDSQDKAVLKGG"
    "PLDGTYRLIQFHFHWGSLDGQGSEHTVDKKKYAAELHLVHWNTKYGDFGKAVQQPDGLAVLGIFLKVGSAKPGLQKVVDVLDS"
    "IKTKGKSADFTNFDPRGLLPESLDYWTYPGSLTTPPLLECVTWIVLKEPISVSSEQVLKFRKLNFNGEGEPEELMVDNWRPAQ"
    "PLKNRQIKASFK"
)

payload = {
    "queries": {
        "ca2_acetazolamide": {
            "chains": [
                {"molecule_type": "protein", "chain_ids": ["A"], "sequence": ca2_sequence},
                {"molecule_type": "ligand",  "chain_ids": ["B"], "smiles": "[Zn+2]"},
                {"molecule_type": "ligand",  "chain_ids": ["C"], "smiles": "CC(=O)Nc1nnc(s1)S(=O)(=O)N"},
            ]
        }
    }
}

Protein sequences in these examples are from UniProt (P0CG48, P00918). You submit and read this request the same way as the ubiquitin example. For complexes like this one, prediction quality depends heavily on providing an MSA, as the next sections show.

Run predictions in parallel on multi-GPU instances

A single OpenFold3 prediction runs on one GPU, so a multi-GPU instance doesn’t make an individual prediction faster. Instead, you can run several predictions at once. On a multi-GPU instance such as ml.g6.12xlarge, which has four GPUs, the container assigns each concurrent request its own GPU. To use all the GPUs, set max_concurrent_invocations_per_instance to the number of GPUs on the instance (four, for ml.g6.12xlarge):

multi_gpu_builder = ModelBuilder.from_jumpstart_config(
    jumpstart_config=JumpStartConfig(
        model_id="huggingface-proteinfolding-openfold3",
        accept_eula=True,
    ),
    compute=Compute(instance_type="ml.g6.12xlarge"),
)
multi_gpu_model = multi_gpu_builder.build()

async_config = AsyncInferenceConfig(
    output_path=f"s3://{bucket}/{prefix}/output",
    failure_path=f"s3://{bucket}/{prefix}/failure",
    max_concurrent_invocations_per_instance=4,   # = number of GPUs on the instance
)

multi_gpu_endpoint = multi_gpu_builder.deploy(inference_config=async_config)

This creates a second endpoint, so remember to delete it as well when you’re done (see Clean up).

In our tests, four concurrent predictions each ran on a separate GPU, with throughput gains that grew with protein size. For larger proteins, the cost per prediction that we measured on ml.g6.12xlarge, based on On-Demand instance pricing, was close to that of ml.g6.4xlarge. Your results depend on your inputs and Region. For pricing, see Amazon SageMaker AI pricing.

Note: ml.g6.12xlarge capacity can be limited. If it isn’t available in your Region, you can increase throughput by scaling out across several ml.g6.4xlarge instances with the autoscaling configuration described later in this post.

Use the following table to choose an instance:

WorkloadRecommended instanceWhy
Interactive exploration by a single userml.g6.2xlarge or ml.g6.4xlargeOne GPU handles one prediction at a time at the lowest hourly cost of the supported instances
Team use or bursts of concurrent requestsml.g6.12xlarge with max_concurrent_invocations_per_instance=4Four predictions run in parallel instead of queuing
High-throughput screeningml.g6.12xlarge with autoscalingHighest throughput per instance of the supported instances. Scales out with queue depth and back to zero

Improve prediction accuracy with your own MSAs

OpenFold3 can take a multiple sequence alignment (MSA) as an additional input for each protein chain. An MSA is a set of evolutionarily related sequences aligned to your query. Co-variation across those sequences signals which residues are likely to be in contact, so MSAs can substantially improve accuracy for many proteins and complexes.

To help keep your sequences within your AWS account, the JumpStart endpoint runs with network isolation and doesn’t call external MSA servers. Instead, it accepts precomputed MSAs in the request. You generate alignments with the pipeline and sequence databases you already use, on infrastructure you control, and pass them to the endpoint. This design can help drug discovery programs that need to keep proprietary sequences private.

If you don’t supply an MSA, the endpoint predicts from the sequence alone. That can work well for small, well-characterized proteins such as ubiquitin. For most real-world targets and complexes, include an MSA. The rest of this section shows how, and how much it improves results.

Bring your own MSA

Each protein chain accepts a precomputed_msa field: a list of alignments, each with a name and the alignment content in A3M or Stockholm format. For a single merged alignment, such as the output of a ColabFold MMseqs2 search, use the name colabfold_main:

with open("ca2_colabfold.a3m") as f:
    ca2_msa = f.read()

payload["queries"]["ca2_acetazolamide"]["chains"][0]["precomputed_msa"] = [
    {"name": "colabfold_main", "content": ca2_msa}
]

This example has one protein chain. If a query has several different protein chains, compute an MSA for each one and attach it to that chain’s precomputed_msa field. Identical copies listed together under one chain_ids entry, such as a homodimer, share a single MSA.

The endpoint also accepts other alignment names, such as uniref90_hits, mgnify_hits, and bfd_uniclust_hits, if you generate MSAs with a different pipeline. Because the request is staged in S3, you can send large alignments. In our tests, alignments of several megabytes worked.

You can generate MSAs with tools such as ColabFold (MMseqs2) or HHblits or JackHMMER. To help keep proprietary sequences inside your environment, run the search on your own AWS infrastructure against locally hosted sequence databases, rather than sending sequences to a public server. For example, ColabFold’s colabfold_batch command uses the public ColabFold MSA server by default, so for proprietary sequences, use colabfold_search with locally hosted databases instead.

How much difference does an MSA make?

We folded the carbonic anhydrase II, zinc, and acetazolamide complex from the previous section twice on the same endpoint: once in single-sequence mode, and once with an MSA from a ColabFold MMseqs2 search.

Metric (first of 5 samples)Without MSAWith MSA
Average pLDDT3098
pTM0.220.98
ipTM0.490.98
Zinc–His94/His96/His119 distance2.3–9.4 Å2.0 Å each
Acetazolamide nitrogen–zinc distance5.6 Å2.0 Å
Prediction time~1.5 minutes~1.5 minutes

With the MSA, OpenFold3 recovers the known binding mode. The zinc ion is coordinated by the three active-site histidines, and the acetazolamide sulfonamide nitrogen binds directly to the zinc, matching the experimental structure. Without the MSA, the protein fold has low confidence and the binding site isn’t formed. Adding the MSA didn’t noticeably change prediction time.

Figure 2: The same carbonic anhydrase II, zinc, and acetazolamide query folded without an MSA (left) and with an MSA (right). Each prediction is colored by pLDDT and superimposed on the experimental crystal structure (gray, PDB 3HS4; Sippel et al., 2009).

Superimposed on the crystal structure, the MSA-based prediction matches it closely: the protein backbone deviates by 0.2 Å (Cα RMSD), the zinc ion by less than 0.1 Å, and the acetazolamide heavy atoms by 0.4 Å RMSD. The single-sequence prediction is misfolded, with a Cα RMSD of 22 Å.

Figure 3: Close-up of the binding site in the MSA-based prediction. The predicted zinc ion (purple) is coordinated by His94, His96, and His119 and by the sulfonamide nitrogen of acetazolamide (green). The crystal pose (gray) is almost entirely hidden behind the prediction.

Carbonic anhydrase II with acetazolamide is one of the most extensively studied complexes in the Protein Data Bank, and closely related structures are likely part of OpenFold3’s training data. Treat this example as a demonstration of the workflow and of how much an MSA matters, not as a benchmark of accuracy on novel targets.

When you compare OpenFold3 results against other tools or published benchmarks, compare like with like: single-sequence results with single-sequence results, and MSA-based results with MSA-based results.

Help reduce cost: Scale to zero when idle

Asynchronous endpoints can scale down to zero instances when no requests are queued, and scale back up when new requests arrive. This pattern suits structure prediction work, which often runs in bursts.

aas = boto3.client("application-autoscaling")
resource_id = f"endpoint/{endpoint_name}/variant/AllTraffic"

aas.register_scalable_target(
    ServiceNamespace="sagemaker",
    ResourceId=resource_id,
    ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount",
    MinCapacity=0,
    MaxCapacity=4,
)

# Scale out and in to keep about 4 queued requests per instance
aas.put_scaling_policy(
    PolicyName="openfold3-backlog",
    ServiceNamespace="sagemaker",
    ResourceId=resource_id,
    ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount",
    PolicyType="TargetTrackingScaling",
    TargetTrackingScalingPolicyConfiguration={
        "TargetValue": 4.0,
        "CustomizedMetricSpecification": {
            "MetricName": "ApproximateBacklogSizePerInstance",
            "Namespace": "AWS/SageMaker",
            "Dimensions": [{"Name": "EndpointName", "Value": endpoint_name}],
            "Statistic": "Average",
        },
        "ScaleInCooldown": 600,
        "ScaleOutCooldown": 300,
    },
)

Target tracking scales the endpoint down to zero after the queue has been empty for a while. In our tests, that took about 15–20 minutes. However, target tracking doesn’t scale the endpoint back up from zero. To start an instance when a request arrives and no instances are running, add a step-scaling policy that’s triggered by the HasBacklogWithoutCapacity metric:

cw = boto3.client("cloudwatch")

step = aas.put_scaling_policy(
    PolicyName="openfold3-scale-from-zero",
    ServiceNamespace="sagemaker",
    ResourceId=resource_id,
    ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount",
    PolicyType="StepScaling",
    StepScalingPolicyConfiguration={
        "AdjustmentType": "ChangeInCapacity",
        "MetricAggregationType": "Average",
        "Cooldown": 300,
        "StepAdjustments": [{"MetricIntervalLowerBound": 0, "ScalingAdjustment": 1}],
    },
)

cw.put_metric_alarm(
    AlarmName=f"{endpoint_name}-has-backlog-without-capacity",
    Namespace="AWS/SageMaker",
    MetricName="HasBacklogWithoutCapacity",
    Dimensions=[{"Name": "EndpointName", "Value": endpoint_name}],
    Statistic="Average",
    Period=60,
    EvaluationPeriods=2,
    DatapointsToAlarm=2,
    Threshold=1,
    ComparisonOperator="GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold",
    TreatMissingData="missing",
    AlarmActions=[step["PolicyARN"]],
)

When a request arrives at an endpoint with zero instances, it waits in the queue while an instance starts. The first request after scaling from zero will take longer to complete as it includes time for the alarm to trigger, the instance to start, plus the prediction itself. Later requests in the same burst run at normal speed. This trade-off can work well for batch workloads. For interactive use, set MinCapacity=1 to keep one instance warm. For more details, see Autoscale an asynchronous endpoint.

Clean up

To stop incurring charges, delete the resources you created when you’re finished. If you configured autoscaling, remove it first: delete the Amazon CloudWatch alarm, then deregister the scalable target. Then delete each endpoint, its endpoint configuration, and its model, including the multi-GPU endpoint if you deployed it:

# 1. If you configured autoscaling, remove it before deleting the endpoint
cw.delete_alarms(AlarmNames=[f"{endpoint_name}-has-backlog-without-capacity"])
aas.deregister_scalable_target(
    ServiceNamespace="sagemaker",
    ResourceId=resource_id,
    ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount",
)

# 2. Delete the endpoints, endpoint configurations, and models
#    (include only the ones you deployed)
from sagemaker.core.resources import EndpointConfig

for m, ep in ((model, endpoint), (multi_gpu_model, multi_gpu_endpoint)):
    endpoint_config = EndpointConfig.get(endpoint_config_name=ep.endpoint_name)
    m.delete()
    ep.delete()
    endpoint_config.delete()

If you no longer need the request and result objects, you can also delete them from s3://<bucket>/openfold3-async/.

Conclusion

With OpenFold3 on SageMaker JumpStart, research and drug discovery teams can deploy an open, inspectable structure prediction model into their own AWS account with a few lines of code. Asynchronous inference handles long-running folds and bursty batch workloads, and multi-GPU instances run predictions in parallel. Network isolation helps you keep proprietary sequences private, and because you can bring your own MSAs, you can benefit from MSAs without sending sequences to an external server. With scale-to-zero, you stop paying for endpoint instances after the queue has been empty long enough for the endpoint to scale in. Other charges, such as for Amazon S3 storage, still apply.

The code in this post is sample code for experimentation. Before you use it with proprietary or regulated data, work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements.

To get started, search for OpenFold3 in SageMaker JumpStart, or open the example notebook from the model card. To learn more about the features used in this post, see Asynchronous inference and Autoscale an asynchronous endpoint. To discuss your structural biology workloads, contact your AWS account team.

About the authors

item.title: Cost-optimizing AssemblyAI speech-to-text inference on AWS w…
item.description: Full title: Cost-optimizing AssemblyAI speech-to-text inference on AWS with Amazon EC2 Spot
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Cost-optimizing AssemblyAI speech-to-text inference on AWS with Amazon EC2 Spot

Speech-to-text inference is computationally intensive. Each audio file triggers a pipeline of deep learning models (acoustic models, language models, and post-processing stages) running on NVIDIA GPUs to meet latency requirements. At scale, this means thousands of GPU instances running continuously.

AssemblyAI needed a way to run GPU-intensive inference workloads cost-effectively at scale, without sacrificing the availability and latency guarantees their customers depend on. Running entirely on On-Demand Instances would be cost-prohibitive. Spot Instances offer significant savings, while Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) can reclaim them with a 2-minute warning when capacity is needed elsewhere. AssemblyAI needed an architecture that absorbs Spot interruptions gracefully while maintaining service level agreement (SLA) commitments. Additionally, customers in regulated industries, including healthcare, finance, and legal, must keep audio data within specific geographic boundaries. They implement strict data residency configurations in European AWS Regions.

Available on AWS Marketplace, AssemblyAI provides an API for transcription, speaker detection, sentiment analysis, chapter detection, and personally identifiable information (PII) redaction. Their models transcribe and analyze speech for high-volume workloads across industries including technology, media, healthcare, and financial services.

In this post, we show you how AssemblyAI runs cost-optimized AI inference at scale for their speech-to-text platform. The architecture uses Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) Spot Instances, and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). Together, these services combine a flexible fleet of NVIDIA GPUs, ECS capacity providers, and a queue-based retry mechanism. The result is significant cost savings while maintaining SLA commitments across European AWS Regions.

Solution overview

AssemblyAI’s inference platform runs on Amazon ECS with compute capacity managed through ECS capacity providers. The fleet mixes Amazon EC2 Spot Instances and On-Demand Instances across multiple NVIDIA GPU instance families, running a single inference model per GPU at a scale of thousands of instances. The architecture is built on four pillars that work together to deliver cost-optimized and resilient inference:

  • Amazon ECS capacity providers mixing Spot and On-Demand.
  • Multi-family GPU Spot diversification across EC2 instance types (such as g4dn.xlarge, g4dn.2xlarge, g5.xlarge, g5.4xlarge, and g6.2xlarge).
  • Queue-based retry architecture using Amazon SQS for interruption recovery.
  • Regional deployment across US West (Oregon) us-west-2 and Europe (London) eu-west-2 for data residency compliance.

The following diagram illustrates how this solution is deployed:

Figure 1: AssemblyAI’s inference architecture on Amazon ECS with Amazon EC2 Spot GPU instances and an Amazon SQS-based retry mechanism

An Amazon ECS cluster runs within a virtual private cloud (VPC) across multiple Availability Zones. The cluster hosts GPU-backed ECS tasks (shown as ECS Task, GPU Spot 1 and ECS Task GPU Spot 2) that poll the queue and process inference jobs. Each task retrieves audio files from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and writes the completed transcription to a results store, which AssemblyAI configures to deliver the output to the end customer.

When a Spot Instance receives an interruption notice, Amazon EventBridge invokes the Spot Interruption Handler (an AWS Lambda function). The handler returns the in-flight job to the Main Job SQS Queue so another healthy ECS task can pick it up. Customers configure their system to route jobs that exhaust retry attempts to a Dead Letter SQS Queue for investigation. Amazon CloudWatch Metrics monitors the health of the fleet and the Spot interruption events, providing observability across the system.

Amazon ECS capacity providers and Spot diversification

To optimize inference costs without compromising reliability, AssemblyAI configures multiple capacity providers in a single capacity provider strategy within each ECS cluster. An On-Demand capacity provider serves as an always-on baseline, and a Spot capacity provider spans different GPU instance families and Availability Zones to serve spikes of demand. Each capacity provider associates with an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group. Amazon ECS managed scaling automates the scaling of GPU instances based on the capacity provider weights and the pending inference tasks. When the task queue grows, the Spot capacity provider requests additional instances from the diversified pool. When demand drops, instances scale in gracefully.

One of the most effective Spot best practices is to be flexible across a wide range of instance types to increase the chances of getting the aggregate compute capacity needed. Rather than depending on a single GPU instance family, AssemblyAI’s infrastructure spans three Amazon EC2 GPU instance families:

  • g4dn instances – Powered by NVIDIA T4 GPUs, providing a cost-effective baseline for standard speech recognition models.
  • g5 instances – Equipped with NVIDIA A10G GPUs, delivering higher throughput for more demanding model architectures.
  • g6 instances – Featuring NVIDIA L4 GPUs, offering improved performance-per-dollar for larger models including large language model-based inference.

By spreading demand across instance families and sizes, AssemblyAI draws from a significantly larger pool of available Spot capacity. Using the price-capacity optimized allocation strategy, Amazon EC2 provisions instances from the Spot capacity pools with the highest available capacity at the lowest price, reducing the likelihood of interruptions.

Queue-based retry for interruption resilience

Maintaining quality of service during Spot interruptions was a core design requirement. AssemblyAI decouples job submission from execution using Amazon SQS. When a transcription request arrives, it’s placed into an Amazon SQS queue. Amazon ECS tasks running on GPU instances poll the queue, pull jobs, and execute the inference pipeline. Individual jobs typically take between 15 seconds and several minutes depending on audio length.

When a Spot Instance receives a 2-minute interruption notice, the retry flow works as follows:

  • In-flight jobs that can complete within the 2-minute window finish normally. Jobs that need more time are returned to the Amazon SQS queue, where they become immediately available for other workers.
  • Another healthy GPU instance picks up the message, potentially on a different instance type or in a different Availability Zone, and completes the inference.

To reduce recovery time, AssemblyAI creates custom Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) containing model artifacts and container images in approximately 2 minutes. For end customers, the impact of a Spot interruption is a small increase in processing time, but the transcription completes successfully and is delivered as expected.

Regional deployment for data residency

Running in multiple AWS Regions allows AssemblyAI to support customers in regulated industries, including healthcare, financial services, and legal services, where audio data must never leave specific geographic boundaries. Each AWS Region runs a fully independent copy of the inference architecture: its own Amazon SQS queues, Amazon ECS clusters, capacity providers, and GPU fleets. Multiple GPU instance families (g4dn, g5, g6) are available in these European Regions with competitive Spot pricing. This instance diversity supports a reliable Spot-based inference service while meeting strict data residency requirements.

Results

By running Amazon EC2 Spot Instances with GPUs in production, AssemblyAI achieved 70 percent cost savings on inference compute compared to On-Demand pricing. As the platform grew nearly 4x year-over-year in compute demand, the Spot-based architecture kept unit economics sustainable. Operating at this scale, AssemblyAI learned that diversifying across instance families and sizes is the most effective lever for minimizing Spot interruption rates. The g4dn, g5, and g6 families tap into independent capacity pools, so when one family experiences capacity pressure, the others remain available. Designing fault tolerance from day one with queue-based retries and fast warm-up turns Spot interruptions into routine events while maintaining SLA commitments.

Conclusion

Teams running batch or near real-time AI workloads with similar characteristics (short-lived, independently retriable jobs on GPU compute) can apply this pattern. Start by diversifying instance families and building queue-based fault tolerance to take advantage of cost-effective Spot infrastructure without compromising availability.

To get started with GPU tasks on Amazon ECS, see Amazon ECS for GPU workloads. To evaluate Spot availability for your workload, explore using Spot placement scores for accelerated compute and Amazon EC2 Spot Instances best practices. AssemblyAI’s Speech-to-Text API is available on AWS Marketplace. To learn more about their platform, visit assemblyai.com.

About the authors

item.title: Cost attribution and controls for AI developer and productiv…
item.description: Full title: Cost attribution and controls for AI developer and productivity tools on Amazon Bedrock
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Cost attribution and controls for AI developer and productivity tools on Amazon Bedrock

Amazon Bedrock provides built-in, zero-instrumentation cost attribution that traces every inference call back to the IAM principal that made it. The identity flows along with organizational tags, into AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0) and AWS Cost Explorer while keeping data inside the AWS security boundary. This post shows you how to use these capabilities to answer three questions that every FinOps and AI Platform leader asks as AI tool adoption scales: What is the real per-user cost? Which teams generate the most spend, and does that spend correlate with the value they deliver? How should next year’s budget scale with headcount and adoption?

The approach works identically regardless of which AI coding or productivity tool makes the call. Claude Code, Claude Desktop, OpenAI Codex, ChatGPT Work, and OpenCode all invoke Amazon Bedrock through one of two inference endpoints: bedrock-runtime or bedrock-mantle, and Bedrock’s attribution mechanism operates at the endpoint layer, beneath any tool-specific logic. You configure identity propagation once, and every tool that routes inference through Bedrock inherits per-user cost visibility automatically.

By the end of this post, you will have AWS IAM Identity Center configured with your external identity provider for per-user attribution, session tags (team, cost center) flowing into CUR 2.0, Amazon Athena queries and dashboard options for ongoing cost visibility, and a clear understanding of Bedrock-native usage controls to enforce spending limits.

How Amazon Bedrock attribution works

Amazon Bedrock records the IAM identity of every inference caller with no changes required to your API calls. When a user invokes a model through either the bedrock-runtime or bedrock-mantle endpoint, Bedrock captures the caller’s full IAM ARN, including the session name for federated users and publishes it to CUR 2.0 in the line_item_iam_principal column. In billing data, usage is aggregated per principal and per usage type for each export interval: one hour in an hourly export, one day in a daily export. CUR does not contain per-request cost. For per-prompt detail, use model invocation logs or request metadata tagging.

Optionally, you can attach tags to IAM principals or pass session tags during federation to add organizational dimensions. These tags appear in CUR 2.0 with the iamPrincipal/ prefix and in Cost Explorer as filterable dimensions. The mechanism supports four access patterns: IAM users, per-application roles, federated identities, and large language model (LLM) gateways proxying to Bedrock. For a comparison of all four, see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock. This post follows the federated identity pattern, which is the natural fit for AI coding and productivity tools where each developer or knowledge worker authenticates individually.

Amazon Bedrock offers additional attribution mechanisms beyond IAM principal tracking that organizations can layer depending on their needs (see Appendix A for a comparison). With Application Inference Profiles, you can tag spend by workload on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. With Projects and Workspaces, you can isolate and tag spend on the bedrock-mantle endpoint. Per-request metadata tagging provides per-prompt token-level detail in model invocation logs for workloads that need granularity finer than finer than CUR 2.0’s per-usage-type aggregation per export interval. You can combine these, for example, IAM principal attribution for per-user dollars on your invoice alongside per-request metadata tags for per-prompt detail in logs. The choice depends on your goal (see Track usage and costs in Amazon Bedrock).

The attribution problem

The developer and productivity tools run on each user’s machine and call Amazon Bedrock directly, or through an LLM gateway. Users authenticate by assuming a shared IAM role, so every API call appears as assumed-role/<role>/<session-name> in billing. If every user assumes the role with the same fixed session name, or calls go through a gateway’s own role, CUR aggregates spend to a single principal. With IAM Identity Center, the session name is the user’s sign-in name, so each user gets their own principal. You can further enrich it with session tags (team, cost center, project). These fields flow into CUR 2.0’s line_item_iam_principal column and cost allocation tags with the iamPrincipal/ prefix, making per-user spend queryable alongside the dollars, with zero changes to your Bedrock API calls.

Claude Platform on AWS and Claude for Enterprise route inference through Anthropic-managed infrastructure. For Claude Platform on AWS, usage is visible by workspace and API key in Anthropic’s admin console, and workspace tags flow to AWS billing. For Claude for Enterprise, per-user usage is visible in Anthropic’s admin console and Usage and Cost API. Spend limits are enforced natively by Anthropic.

Prerequisites

Before starting, make sure you have:

  • An AWS account with IAM permissions to access Bedrock models you intend to use.
  • AWS IAM Identity Center enabled in your management account.
  • An external identity provider (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, or Ping Identity) with SCIM provisioning capability.
  • AWS CLI v2 configured on developer machines.
  • AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR 2.0) enabled with IAM principal data and delivered to an S3 bucket.
  • Cost allocation tags activated from the management (payer) account.
  • An Athena table configured to query CUR 2.0 data (see the GitHub sample to get started).

Step 1: Configure IAM Identity Center with your external IdP

Configure your external identity provider as the identity source in AWS IAM Identity Center. Navigate to IAM Identity Center → Settings → Identity source → Change identity source. Select “External identity provider” and configure SAML 2.0 or SCIM connectivity with your IdP. Enable SCIM provisioning to automatically synchronize users and groups, including organizational attributes like team and department.

Configure attribute mapping for session tags by navigating to Settings → Attributes for access control. Map your IdP’s organizational attributes to session tags that will flow into CUR 2.0. These attributes propagate as session tags (aws:PrincipalTag/Team, aws:PrincipalTag/CostCenter) on every API call the user makes, including every Bedrock invocation through both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints.

Step 2: Create a permission set for Bedrock access

Create a permission set in Identity Center that grants Bedrock invocation access. Each user gets their own session within this permission set. This is the foundation of per-user attribution. The specific IAM actions depend on which Bedrock endpoint the tool calls.

Tools that call the bedrock-mantle endpoint (such as Codex and ChatGPT Work) require bedrock-mantle:CreateInference and related actions scoped to a Project resource. Tools that call the bedrock-runtime endpoint (such as Claude Code and Claude Desktop) require bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream scoped to the relevant foundation model or inference profile ARNs. You can combine both in a single permission set if your organization uses tools across both endpoints.

{
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Sid": "BedrockMantleAccess",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "bedrock-mantle:CreateInference",
                "bedrock-mantle:CountTokens"
            ],
            "Resource": “arn:aws:bedrock-mantle:::project/”
        },
        {
            "Sid": "BedrockModelAccess",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "bedrock:InvokeModel",
                "bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream",
                "bedrock:ListInferenceProfiles",
                "bedrock:GetInferenceProfile"
            ],
			“Resource”: [
			“arn:aws:bedrock:::inference-profile/“,
			“arn:aws:bedrock:::application-inference-profile/“,
			“arn:aws:bedrock:::foundation-model/”
			]
        }
    ]
}

Note: These resource patterns are a starting point. Narrow them to the specific inference profiles and Projects that you approve. Assign this permission set to the relevant groups synchronized from your IdP. Policy changes are instant and universal, audit is centralized through AWS CloudTrail with each user’s identity, and users do not receive long-lived AWS credentials.

Step 3: Configure user workstations

Users configure their AWS CLI profile once, no custom scripts, credential helpers, or browser automation required. The following ~/.aws/config entry establishes the SSO session:

[profile bedrock]
sso_session = corp
sso_account_id = 111122223333
sso_role_name = BedrockDeveloperAccess
region = us-east-1

[sso-session corp]
sso_start_url = https://your-org.awsapps.com/start
sso_region = us-east-1
sso_registration_scopes = sso:account:access

Users authenticate by running aws sso login --profile bedrock, which opens the browser, authenticates through the IdP, and caches credentials locally. The AWS CLI and SDKs refresh the access token automatically until the IAM Identity Center session ends (8 hours by default). The core trade-off in configuring session duration is between security posture and operational convenience.

Step 4: Point tools at Amazon Bedrock

Each AI tool needs only a standard configuration change to route inference through Bedrock. Because Bedrock attribution operates at the endpoint layer, no tool-specific instrumentation is required. The tool authenticates using the AWS credential chain established in Step 3, and Bedrock captures the caller identity automatically.

Claude Desktop reads third-party inference settings from OS-native managed preferences (/Library/Managed Preferences/com.anthropic.claudefordesktop.plist on macOS, HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Claude on Windows). Author the configuration once in the in-app window (Developer → Configure Third-Party Inference) and choose Export to produce a .mobileconfig or .reg for your mobile device management (MDM) system. For per-user attribution, use in-app AWS sign-in, each user authenticates against IAM Identity Center inside the application, with no AWS CLI on the device:

inferenceProvider bedrock
inferenceBedrockRegion us-east-1
inferenceBedrockSsoStartUrl https://your-org.awsapps.com/start
inferenceBedrockSsoRegion us-east-1
inferenceBedrockSsoAccountId 111122223333
inferenceBedrockSsoRoleName BedrockDeveloperAccess
inferenceModels ["us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5","us.anthropic.claude-opus-5"]

Configuration is read at launch. Users must quit and reopen the application. If developers already run AWS CLI v2, set inferenceBedrockProfile instead and the app runs aws sso login for them.

Claude Code CLI reads the standard AWS SDK credential chain, including SSO profiles. If AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK is set, Claude Code authenticates with that key and does not use the credential chain, so calls are attributed to the IAM user behind the key. Disable it when you want per-user SSO attribution.

Set awsAuthRefresh in the settings file to automatically re-authenticate when credentials expire:

{
    "awsAuthRefresh": "aws sso login --profile bedrock",
    "env": {
        "CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK": "1",
        "AWS_PROFILE": "bedrock",
        "AWS_REGION": "us-east-1"
    }
}

Pin model versions before fleet rollout so a new release doesn’t change what users invoke:

export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL='us.anthropic.claude-opus-5'
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL='us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5'

Codex and ChatGPT Work read ~/.codex/config.toml. Both the desktop app and CLI consume the same configuration layers. For the bedrock-mantle endpoint:

model_provider = "amazon-bedrock"
model = "openai.gpt-5.6-sol"

[model_providers.amazon-bedrock.aws]
region = "us-east-1"

For the bedrock-runtime endpoint, use inference profile IDs:

model_provider = "amazon-bedrock-runtime"
model = "us.openai.gpt-5.6-sol"
web_search = "disabled"

Set AWS_PROFILE in the environment for both endpoints. For the desktop app, place environment variables in ~/.codex/.env since desktop applications may not inherit shell environment variables. If AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK is set, Codex uses it before the SSO profile and calls are attributed to the IAM user behind that API key. Unset it when you want per-user SSO attribution.

Step 5: Enable cost attribution in CUR 2.0

From the AWS Billing Console (Billing → Data Exports → Create export), configure delivery to S3 in Parquet format with hourly or daily granularity. Select “Include caller identity (IAM principal) allocation data” to populate the line_item_iam_principal column. Bedrock’s IAM principal cost tracking works for both bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints.

Creating the export in the management account captures all accounts’ Bedrock usage. If you created a CUR 2.0 data export before IAM principal attribution launched, you must create a new export with the caller identity option selected.

Activate cost allocation tags after users have signed in and made at least one Bedrock call. Tags appear in Billing only after the principal has made a call. In the management account, open Billing → Cost allocation tags, filter by type IAM principal, and activate Team and CostCenter:

aws ce update-cost-allocation-tags-status \
--cost-allocation-tags-status TagKey=Team,Status=Active
aws ce update-cost-allocation-tags-status \
--cost-allocation-tags-status TagKey=CostCenter,Status=Active

Allow up to 24 hours for tags to appear and up to 48 hours to see them in CUR 2.0 and Cost Explorer. Activation is not retroactive. Bedrock meters and bills input, output, cache-read, and cache-write tokens separately. A single hour of activity under one IAM principal typically produces four CUR rows.

Step 6: Query cost data with Amazon Athena

Once CUR 2.0 is delivered to S3 and an Athena table is configured, query usage and cost at your desired granularity. The following query extracts per-user cost:

SELECT
  regexp_extract(line_item_iam_principal, 'assumed-role/[^/]+/(.+)$', 1) AS user_name,
  line_item_usage_type,
  SUM(line_item_unblended_cost) AS total_cost_usd,
  SUM(line_item_usage_amount)   AS usage_units
FROM cur_table
WHERE line_item_product_code IN ('AmazonBedrock', 'AmazonBedrockService')
  AND line_item_iam_principal IS NOT NULL
  AND line_item_line_item_type = 'Usage'
  AND billing_period = '2026-09'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY total_cost_usd DESC;

For daily spend trend per cost center:

SELECT
    DATE(line_item_usage_start_date) AS usage_date,
    element_at(tags, 'iamPrincipal/CostCenter') AS cost_center,
    SUM(line_item_unblended_cost) AS daily_cost_usd
FROM cur_table
WHERE line_item_product_code IN ('AmazonBedrock', 'AmazonBedrockService')
    AND line_item_iam_principal IS NOT NULL
    AND line_item_line_item_type = 'Usage'
    AND billing_period = '2026-09'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, daily_cost_usd DESC;

Athena charges by data scanned. Columnar Parquet and the billing_period filter keep queries inexpensive.

Step 7: Visualization

AWS Cost Explorer requires zero setup. Group by tags once they are activated. AWS Quick Sight connects to Athena for interactive dashboards with anomaly detection that alerts on unexpected spend spikes. You can integrate with the CUDOS dashboard, an open-source Cloud Intelligence Dashboards (CID) framework that provides detailed cost insights. Grafana with the Athena plugin renders CUR data as time series alongside existing infrastructure metrics.

Implementing per-user usage controls

Once per-user cost visibility is established through IAM principal attribution in CUR 2.0, organizations need enforcement mechanisms to help prevent uncontrolled accumulation. Numerous approaches exist today, each trading enforcement latency against operational complexity.

AWS Budgets with budget actions is the lightest option requiring no custom infrastructure. Set a budget threshold filtered by IAM principal tags, and attach an action (such as applying a deny policy) that triggers when the threshold is breached. The trade-off: AWS Budgets updates up to three times a day, and Bedrock charges can take up to 24 hours to appear in billing data, so a high-velocity user can overshoot by up to a day before enforcement takes effect.

Amazon CloudWatch alarms and AWS Lambda offer near-real-time enforcement using Bedrock’s native CloudWatch metrics (InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, Invocations) filtered by model ID or inference profile. Enforcement latency drops to 1–5 minutes. To get user-level granularity with this approach, use Application Inference Profiles or per-user roles.

Amazon DynamoDB-based quota tracking enforces limits at the authentication layer. A Lambda function increments per-user token counters in DynamoDB and withholds credentials once a limit is exceeded. Enforcement takes effect at the next credential refresh, not on individual API calls, but removes the billing-data lag inherent in budget-based approaches.

LLM gateway proxy delivers per-invocation blocking across Bedrock models and SDK workloads, at the cost of highest operational complexity and added latency on every request. See Multi-Provider Generative AI Gateway.

Organizations typically layer these options: CUR 2.0 for reporting, a gateway or DynamoDB-based enforcement for real-time control, and AWS Budgets as a backstop. For the full reference, see How to limit usage and cost on Amazon Bedrock.

Conclusion

Amazon Bedrock’s IAM principal attribution gives you per-user cost tracking for every AI developer and productivity tool that routes inference through Bedrock, with no custom credential scripts, per-user IAM roles, or additional infrastructure. Users authenticate with aws sso login, the same flow they use for other AWS access, and every Bedrock invocation automatically carries their identity into billing data.

Each component can be adopted incrementally. Start by connecting your IdP to Identity Center and assigning a Bedrock permission set to get session-level attribution in CloudTrail immediately. Activate cost allocation tags to surface that data in CUR 2.0. Add Athena queries and dashboards as reporting requirements grow. Layer usage controls, from AWS Budgets to real-time gateway enforcement, based on your organization’s tolerance for enforcement latency.

Regardless of which AI tools your organization adopts today or adds tomorrow, the attribution and control mechanisms described here operate at the Bedrock platform layer. Configure once, and every tool that calls Bedrock inherits the governance.

About the authors

item.title: Build a model improvement flywheel with Amazon SageMaker Hyp…
item.description: Full title: Build a model improvement flywheel with Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Data Capture
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Build a model improvement flywheel with Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Data Capture

Foundation models deployed on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod meet inputs that no pre-curated dataset covers: domain-specific jargon, unexpected formats, new products, and changing user behavior. Without a record of production inference data, teams can’t detect drift, find failure patterns, or use real interactions to improve the model.

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now provides Data Capture, a built-in capability that records live inference inputs and outputs to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) at three independent tiers, with minimal latency impact and zero impact on model availability.

In this post, we walk through one complete example on a single SageMaker HyperPod cluster. A home-appliance support router captures its production traffic, Amazon Athena queries surface a new-product blind spot, a SQL policy labels the captured records, and a fine-tune on that data teaches the router the new product. We measure accuracy before and after, on data that could not have existed before the model was deployed. The inference operator serves the model on one node, and the training operator runs the fine-tuning on another.

We use synthetic data for the walkthrough. The scripts, manifests, SQL, synthetic datasets, and expected outputs are available in the accompanying GitHub repository.

Three-tier Data Capture architecture

HyperPod Data Capture provides three independent tiers, each at a different point in the request path. You can turn on any combination in the same dataCapture block.

Tier 1: SageMaker endpointTier 2: Load balancerTier 3: Model pod
What’s capturedFull request/response payloadsApplication Load Balancer (ALB) access-log fields: request line, status codes, timings, client IP, user agentFull request/response payloads plus event metadata
Managed bySageMaker native data captureALB access logsHyperPod inference operator (NGINX + OTel collector + S3 uploader sidecars)
Best forCompliance, Model Monitor, auditTraffic and error-rate monitoring at low costDebugging, analytics, training-data collection
ConfigurationsagemakerEndpoint: — sampling %, input/output, AWS KMSloadBalancer: { enabled: true }modelPod: — sampling %, input/output, buffer, max payload size, AWS KMS, content types

Tiers 1 and 3 both store full payloads, so enabling both stores every record twice. Use Tier 1 for compliance and Model Monitor, Tier 2 when you only need traffic metadata, and Tier 3 when you intend to use the payloads. This post uses Tier 3 only. Because Tier 3 records complete payloads, which can include names, addresses, and order numbers, protect that data before it becomes training data. Use sampling, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption (kmsKeyId), S3 lifecycle rules, and personally identifiable information (PII) redaction (for example, with Amazon Comprehend).

Prerequisites

  • A SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), with the inference operator installed (Setting up your HyperPod clusters for model deployment) and the training operator EKS add-on amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-training-operator installed (Installing the training operator).
  • Two available NVIDIA GPUs, one for serving and one for training. We used an ml.g6e.8xlarge for serving and an ml.g6e.xlarge for training (one 48 GB NVIDIA L40S each). The serving pod holds its GPU for the life of the endpoint, so with only one GPU the training pod stays Pending.
  • kubectl configured for the cluster.
  • An S3 bucket in the same Region.

Confirm both operators are installed. The command returns two rows:

kubectl get crd | grep -E 'inferenceendpointconfigs|hyperpodpytorchjobs'
hyperpodpytorchjobs.sagemaker.amazonaws.com                         2026-09-21T10:57:14Z
inferenceendpointconfigs.inference.sagemaker.aws.amazon.com         2026-08-06T11:58:53Z

Solution overview

The following diagram shows the five steps of the walkthrough on one SageMaker HyperPod cluster: capture every request and response to Amazon S3, analyze the captures with Athena, label them with a SQL policy, fine-tune with the training operator on a second GPU, and redeploy side by side with capture still on.

Figure 1: The five-step flywheel on a single SageMaker HyperPod cluster, from capture through Athena analysis, labeling, fine-tuning, and redeploy

The inference operator adds three sidecars to the model pod. Every request that passes through the NGINX proxy is copied to an OpenTelemetry collector, batched, and written to S3 through a Mountpoint-S3 volume. Athena reads those files in place. The training operator runs the fine-tune as a HyperPodPyTorchJob on a second GPU, and the new model is served by a second endpoint that also has capture on.

Step 0: Set your variables

Every later step reads these. Edit the first block, then paste the whole thing:

# --- edit these ---
export EKS_CLUSTER_NAME="my-hyperpod-eks"
export AWS_REGION="us-east-1"
export BUCKET="amzn-s3-demo-bucket"
export SERVE_INSTANCE_TYPE="ml.g6e.8xlarge"     # node type for the first endpoint
export TRAIN_INSTANCE_TYPE="ml.g6e.xlarge"      # node type for the fine-tuning job
# --- leave as-is ---
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="$AWS_REGION"
export ENDPOINT_NAME="appliance-router"
export MODEL_LOCATION="models/qwen2.5-3b-instruct"
export MODEL_V2_LOCATION="models/qwen2.5-3b-router-v2"
export TRAIN_SA="flywheel"                     # service account with S3 access via EKS Pod Identity
aws eks update-kubeconfig --name "$EKS_CLUSTER_NAME" --region "$AWS_REGION"
render() { python3 -c 'import os,sys; sys.stdout.write(os.path.expandvars(sys.stdin.read()))'; }

Step 1: Stage the base model in S3

We use Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct because it is small enough to fine-tune in about a minute and fits on a single L40S.

pip install -q huggingface_hub
python3 -c "from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download; \
  snapshot_download('Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct', local_dir='qwen2.5-3b-instruct')"
aws s3 sync qwen2.5-3b-instruct "s3://${BUCKET}/${MODEL_LOCATION}/" --exclude ".cache/*"

Step 2: IAM permissions

Four identities need access. For the policy statements, see Data capture for inference on HyperPod.

  • The Mountpoint-S3 CSI driver role. Tier 3 capture writes through a Mountpoint-S3 volume, and the driver authenticates as its own IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) role, not as the pod’s service account. It needs s3:PutObject, s3:AbortMultipartUpload, and s3:DeleteObject on your capture bucket, plus kms:Decrypt, kms:GenerateDataKey, and kms:DescribeKey if you set kmsKeyId. If this is missing, the endpoint stays healthy and requests succeed, but no captures appear. See Mountpoint for Amazon S3 CSI driver.
  • The inference operator execution role. It needs s3:PutObject on your capture bucket, plus kms:Decrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey if you set kmsKeyId. The capture files themselves are written through the CSI driver role, so when no captures appear, check that role first.
  • The training pod’s service account ($TRAIN_SA). Read access to the base model and training data, and write access for the merged model, through EKS Pod Identity.
  • Athena. Read access to the capture prefix, plus a query-results location.

Enabling Data Capture

The next three steps deploy the router with Tier 3 capture on, check that the pod runs the capture sidecars, and confirm that records reach Amazon S3.

Step 3: Deploy the model with Tier 3 capture enabled

This is the whole feature: the dataCapture.modelPod.enabled: true block. Everything else is an ordinary vLLM deployment.

cat > endpoint.yaml <<'YAML'
apiVersion: inference.sagemaker.aws.amazon.com/v1
kind: InferenceEndpointConfig
metadata:
  name: ${ENDPOINT_NAME}
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  modelName: ${ENDPOINT_NAME}
  endpointName: ${ENDPOINT_NAME}
  instanceType: ${SERVE_INSTANCE_TYPE}
  invocationEndpoint: v1/chat/completions
  modelSourceConfig:
    modelSourceType: s3
    modelLocation: ${MODEL_LOCATION}
    s3Storage:
      bucketName: ${BUCKET}
      region: ${AWS_REGION}

  # >>> This is all you need to turn on Tier 3 data capture <<<
  dataCapture:
    s3Uri: "s3://${BUCKET}/capture/"
    modelPod:
      enabled: true
      initialSamplingPercentage: 100
      bufferConfig:
        batchSize: 50
        flushIntervalSeconds: 60
      payloadConfig:
        maxPayloadSizeKB: 1024

  worker:
    image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.10.0
    modelInvocationPort:
      containerPort: 8000
      name: http
    modelVolumeMount:
      mountPath: /opt/ml/model
      name: model-weights
    args: ["--model", "/opt/ml/model", "--served-model-name", "${ENDPOINT_NAME}",
           "--port", "8000", "--max-model-len", "2048", "--gpu-memory-utilization", "0.90"]
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: "2", memory: 16Gi, nvidia.com/gpu: 1 }
      limits:   { nvidia.com/gpu: 1 }
YAML
render < endpoint.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

The preceding modelPod block sets 100% sampling and captures both input and output, which are the defaults. To tune it, add any of these optional fields under modelPod:

modelPod:
  enabled: true
  initialSamplingPercentage: 50          # capture 50% of requests (default 100)
  bufferConfig:
    batchSize: 100                       # records buffered per upload batch (default 10)
    flushIntervalSeconds: 60             # max seconds before a flush (default 60)
  payloadConfig:
    maxPayloadSizeKB: 1024               # truncate payloads larger than this (default: no limit)
  kmsKeyId: "arn:aws:kms:...:key/..."    # encrypt captures at rest

Step 4: Wait for the pod

A capture-enabled pod runs four containers: the model, sidecar-reverse-proxy (NGINX), otel-collector, and s3-uploader. The model container and the pod’s app label are both named after modelName.

kubectl get pods -l app=$ENDPOINT_NAME -o custom-columns=\
'NAME:.metadata.name,READY:.status.containerStatuses[*].ready,CONTAINERS:.spec.containers[*].name,NODE:.spec.nodeName'
NAME                            READY                 CONTAINERS                                                              NODE
appliance-router-849f466476-4f5v8   true,true,true,true   appliance-router,s3-uploader,sidecar-reverse-proxy,otel-collector   hyperpod-i-0f3fe2684afd6a583

In our run, the pod was ready about five minutes after kubectl apply, most of it spent downloading the weights.

Step 5: Send a request and confirm captures land in S3

Send an inference request through the capture proxy on port 8081, then, after the flush interval, list the capture prefix. The model itself listens on port 8000. Requests sent there bypass the proxy and are not captured.

POD=$(kubectl get pod -l app=$ENDPOINT_NAME -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl port-forward "pod/$POD" 18081:8081 >/dev/null 2>&1 &
sleep 5

curl -s http://localhost:18081/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"'"$ENDPOINT_NAME"'","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"my fridge is not cooling"}],"max_tokens":24}'

echo "Waiting for the capture buffer to flush..."; sleep 75
aws s3 ls "s3://${BUCKET}/capture/" --recursive | grep '\.jsonl$' | head
2026-09-28 15:47:14     634356 capture/20e4425092f90c7f/pod/AllTraffic/2026/09/28/15/28-15-47-12-999-ac31d31b-5156-46ad-9ccc-e8a040ab9ab2.jsonl

You see one or more .jsonl objects under {s3Uri}/{uniqueID}/pod/{variant}/{YYYY}/{MM}/{DD}/{HH}/. The uniqueID is generated per endpoint. Each line is one inference in the SageMaker data-capture format shown next.

The captured record format

The request and response bodies are stored base64-encoded, as the encoding field shows, so reading them back requires base64-decoding and then parsing JSON:

{
  "captureData": {
    "endpointInput":  { "observedContentType": "application/json", "mode": "INPUT",
                        "data": "eyJtb2RlbCI6ICJyb3V0ZXItZnJlc2giLCAidGVtcGVyYXR1cmUiOiAwLCAi...", "encoding": "BASE64" },
    "endpointOutput": { "observedContentType": "application/json", "mode": "OUTPUT",
                        "data": "eyJpZCI6ImNoYXRjbXBsLTctMTc5MDYxMDM2OS4wMDUtMjMxMiIsIm9iamVj...", "encoding": "BASE64" }
  },
  "eventMetadata": { "eventId": "26859f07-d60b-4683-94aa-d21e7f19e746", "inferenceTime": "2026-09-28T15:46:09Z" },
  "eventVersion": "0"
}

Decoded, endpointInput.data is the request body the client sent and endpointOutput.data is the response the model returned.

The scenario: A support-ticket router meets a product launch

The deployed model is a support-ticket router for a home-appliance retailer. It uses vLLM guided JSON decoding to classify each ticket into one of six categories: ProductFridge, ProductWasher, ProductOven, ProductDishwasher, ProductMicrowave, or the catch-all Other. Guided decoding means it can only return a valid object with one of those labels:

{"category": "ProductWasher", "confidence": 1}

After the model was deployed, the retailer launched its own line of air conditioners, the Arctis series (Arctis 9K, 12K, Mini, and so on). The router has no category for them. It can’t say “this is new.” It can only pick the closest label it knows. Unless every request and response is recorded, the evidence disappears the moment the response is returned.

The synthetic traffic

We generated two synthetic datasets:

  • Production traffic: 900 tickets, replayed in order through the capture proxy over 15 minutes, using the router’s original six-label prompt. The first 400 come before the launch and mention no air conditioners. In the remaining 500, the share of Arctis tickets ramps from 15% to 55%.
  • Evaluation set: 280 labeled tickets, 40 per category, including the new ProductAC. It is held out by content: it uses symptoms, sentence templates, and Arctis model names that never appear in the traffic.

Each production request looks like this (system prompt abbreviated):

{"model": "appliance-router", "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 40,
 "messages": [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a support-ticket router for a home-appliance retailer. ... category is one of: ProductFridge, ProductWasher, ProductOven, ProductDishwasher, ProductMicrowave, Other. ..."},
              {"role": "user", "content": "Hi, our Arctis 12K blows warm air since last week. Order #66759."}],
 "guided_json": {"type": "object", "required": ["category", "confidence"],
                 "properties": {"category": {"enum": ["ProductFridge", "ProductWasher", "ProductOven",
                                                      "ProductDishwasher", "ProductMicrowave", "Other"]},
                                "confidence": {"type": "number"}}}}

To replay the traffic, clone the accompanying repository, generate the datasets, and send them through the capture proxy. scripts/pod.sh runs the client inside the model container, so no load balancer or DNS is needed. The client prints the three timestamps that the Athena steps use: RUN_START, LAUNCH_TS (the first post-launch ticket), and RUN_END.

git clone https://github.com/awslabs/awsome-distributed-ai.git
cd awsome-distributed-ai/examples/use-cases/sagemaker-hyperpod-data-capture-flywheel
(cd data && python3 ../scripts/gen_dataset.py)
scripts/pod.sh $ENDPOINT_NAME drive /tmp/tickets_traffic.jsonl --seconds 900
RUN_START=2026-09-28 15:52:40
  sent 100/900
...
LAUNCH_TS=2026-09-28 15:59:20
...
RUN_END=2026-09-28 16:07:40

Export the three values that your run printed, and wait one flush interval:

export RUN_START="2026-09-28 15:52:40" LAUNCH_TS="2026-09-28 15:59:20" RUN_END="2026-09-28 16:07:40"
sleep 75    # one flush interval

Surfacing the problem with Amazon Athena

Offline benchmarks still look unchanged after the launch, because they are frozen in the past. The shift is visible only in the captured production traffic. This section shows how a data scientist finds it with Athena, without provisioning any infrastructure.

Step 6: Set your variables and configure an Athena helper function

export ATHENA_DB="flywheel_demo"
export ATHENA_OUTPUT="s3://${BUCKET}/athena-results/"
# Each endpoint writes under its own uniqueID. Pick the prefix whose captured requests name this
# endpoint, not whichever prefix sorts first (the Step 15 endpoint adds a second one).
for id in $(aws s3 ls "s3://${BUCKET}/capture/" | awk '/PRE/{print $2}'); do
  key=$(aws s3 ls "s3://${BUCKET}/capture/${id}pod/AllTraffic/" --recursive | awk '/\.jsonl$/{print $4; exit}')
  [ -n "$key" ] || continue
  model=$(aws s3 cp "s3://${BUCKET}/${key}" - 2>/dev/null | head -n 1 | python3 -c 'import sys, json, base64; r = json.loads(sys.stdin.readline()); print(json.loads(base64.b64decode(r["captureData"]["endpointInput"]["data"]))["model"])')
  if [ "$model" = "$ENDPOINT_NAME" ]; then export CAPTURE_LOCATION="s3://${BUCKET}/capture/${id}pod/AllTraffic/"; break; fi
done
echo "$CAPTURE_LOCATION"     # s3://<bucket>/capture/<uniqueID>/pod/AllTraffic/

# run_athena "<SQL>": runs one statement, prints tab-separated rows, and sets LAST_QID
run_athena() {
  local qid st
  qid=$(aws athena start-query-execution --query-string "$1" \
        --query-execution-context "Database=$ATHENA_DB" \
        --result-configuration "OutputLocation=$ATHENA_OUTPUT" \
        --output text --query 'QueryExecutionId') || return 1
  while :; do
    st=$(aws athena get-query-execution --query-execution-id "$qid" \
         --output text --query 'QueryExecution.Status.State')
    case "$st" in
      SUCCEEDED) break ;;
      FAILED|CANCELLED) aws athena get-query-execution --query-execution-id "$qid" \
          --output text --query 'QueryExecution.Status.StateChangeReason' >&2; return 1 ;;
    esac
    sleep 2
  done
  LAST_QID=$qid
  aws athena get-query-results --query-execution-id "$qid" \
    --output text --query 'ResultSet.Rows[*].Data[*].VarCharValue'
}
run_athena "CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS ${ATHENA_DB}"

Step 7: Declare the captures to Athena (two layers)

The first layer is the envelope. An external table describes the outer JSON of each record, and partition projection over year/month/day/hour maps the hourly S3 prefixes to partitions without a crawler or ADD PARTITION. The data fields are declared as plain strings, because they are base64 text.

run_athena "
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS inference_captures (
  captureData struct<
    endpointInput:  struct<observedContentType: string, mode: string, data: string, encoding: string>,
    endpointOutput: struct<observedContentType: string, mode: string, data: string, encoding: string>
  >,
  eventMetadata struct<eventId: string, inferenceTime: string>,
  eventVersion string
)
PARTITIONED BY (year string, month string, day string, hour string)
ROW FORMAT SERDE 'org.openx.data.jsonserde.JsonSerDe'
LOCATION '${CAPTURE_LOCATION}'
TBLPROPERTIES (
  'projection.enabled'='true',
  'projection.year.type'='integer',  'projection.year.range'='2026,2035',
  'projection.month.type'='integer', 'projection.month.range'='1,12', 'projection.month.digits'='2',
  'projection.day.type'='integer',   'projection.day.range'='1,31',   'projection.day.digits'='2',
  'projection.hour.type'='integer',  'projection.hour.range'='0,23',  'projection.hour.digits'='2',
  'storage.location.template'='${CAPTURE_LOCATION}\${year}/\${month}/\${day}/\${hour}/'
)"

The second layer is a view that decodes each record once. from_utf8(from_base64(...)) turns the payloads back into JSON. Without it, every extraction returns NULL. The ticket is the user message (messages[1], because messages[0] is the system prompt). The model’s answer is a JSON string inside the response JSON, so it needs a second extraction.

run_athena "
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW preds AS
WITH decoded AS (
  SELECT CAST(from_iso8601_timestamp(eventMetadata.inferenceTime) AS timestamp) AS ts,
         from_utf8(from_base64(captureData.endpointInput.data))  AS req,
         from_utf8(from_base64(captureData.endpointOutput.data)) AS resp
  FROM inference_captures
  WHERE year = '${RUN_START:0:4}' AND month = '${RUN_START:5:2}' AND day = '${RUN_START:8:2}'
)
SELECT ts,
       json_extract_scalar(req, '\$.messages[1].content') AS ticket_text,
       json_extract_scalar(json_extract_scalar(resp, '\$.choices[0].message.content'), '\$.category') AS predicted_category,
       CAST(json_extract_scalar(json_extract_scalar(resp, '\$.choices[0].message.content'), '\$.confidence') AS double) AS confidence
FROM decoded
WHERE ts >= timestamp '${RUN_START}' AND ts < timestamp '${RUN_END}'
"
run_athena "SELECT count(*) AS n, count_if(predicted_category IS NULL) AS unparsed FROM preds"
n   unparsed
900 0

Two notes on the view:

  • Always filter on partitions. Athena reads raw JSON, so a query without a partition filter scans every object you have ever captured. The view filters to one day, and the time bound limits it to our traffic run: the same prefix also holds the request from Step 5.
  • messages[1] assumes one system message followed by one user message. Captured traffic is whatever clients actually sent, so adjust the extraction for multi-turn or few-shot requests.

The following chart plots the per-minute share of tickets routed to Other as bars, and the cumulative share as a line, with the launch marked.

Figure 2: Per-minute and cumulative share of tickets routed to Other, before and after the Arctis launch

Before the launch, Other stays under 7% per minute. It jumps to 15% in the launch minute and keeps climbing, reaching 47–65% in the last three minutes. The cumulative line in the chart only reaches 22.6%, because it averages the post-launch tickets with all the traffic from before the launch. That is why the per-minute rate, not the cumulative share, is what you would put behind an alarm.

The Other bucket isn’t a mix of unrelated tickets. It’s dominated by one product name, arctis, and the vocabulary of a cooling appliance, which points to a new category the router has no label for.

Step 10: How big is it, and does the model’s confidence flag it?

Search the whole traffic stream for the new product, not just the Other bucket:

run_athena "
