  • Model invocation response carries a usage block with inputTokens, outputTokens, cacheReadInputTokens, and cacheWriteInputTokens. Accumulating those across the turns of a single task gives you the four terms of the preceding cost-per-attempt formula. One gotcha: when caching is enabled, inputTokens counts only the uncached tokens, so your total input volume is inputTokens + cacheReadInputTokens + cacheWriteInputTokens. Sum them to know the footprint, but price them separately, since the three bill at different rates. Evaluate this multiple times throughout your journey and set the cache checkpoints based on what is the active current load. The drift in cache checkpoints happens as the application progresses and the tools become stale. This means that you will be writing more to the cache in 3 months from now when the drift has happened. Evaluating your data constantly for optimal cache usage becomes a primary lever to reduce cost.
  • Model invocation logging writes per-invocation token counts to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch Logs, so you can measure turns-to-completion against real production traffic instead of a sample. Tag calls with request metadata to slice those logged token counts by team, feature, or experiment. However, these are log fields, not cost allocation tags, and never appear in AWS Cost Explorer or your Cost and Usage Report. Application inference profiles do reach both, at a grain of one usage type per day. That grain is right for chargeback but too coarse for cost per task. Multiplying logged token counts by the published rates gives you a near real-time estimate rather than an invoice. It won’t reflect commitments, batch pricing, or provisioned throughput unless you model them. Reconcile against your Cost and Usage Report before you treat it as the bill.

Reducing cost per task: Four levers

Each of the four drivers has a lever, and each is documented in depth. Prompt caching cuts the re-sent context that made Model A expensive, which makes it the largest win on agentic paths. Intelligent prompt routing sends the easy requests to a cheaper model in the same family. A tool schema plus a maxTokens cap holds verbosity down more reliably than prose instructions do, and extended thinking stays off until a benchmark shows it earns its cost back. Batch inference halves the rate on bulk single-turn work, though it rules out tool calling and multi-turn exchange.

Proving agent ROI: Describe the human baseline

Efficient isn’t the same as valuable. An agent can be perfectly optimized and still not be worth running. The question that decides budgets is: is the agent better than the humans were?

Document the human process first

The biggest mistake in agent ROI is trying to prove value without first describing the human workflow. Before building or scaling an agent, write down the current process in operational terms: what triggers the work, which human roles are involved, where the handoffs sit, how completion is defined. This sounds like bureaucracy. It’s actually measurement design. Every instrumentation decision downstream (what counts as a run, what counts as success, where human time is spent) falls out of this description.

Measure the baseline before the agent ships

With the process described, measure the human baseline over a meaningful window: time to completion, queue time, active effort, reopen rate, escalation rate, cost per task, and outcome quality. Baselines must be measured before the agent goes live, not reconstructed from memory after the fact. Retrospective baselines are systematically flattering to the agent: people remember the average case and forget the fast ones.

Instrument the workflow as an experiment

After the baseline exists, instrument the agent workflow as an experiment from day one. Every run gets a trace ID, and every meaningful step is observable. A workflow-run record aggregates everything above the model call into a single analyzable unit:

{
  "runId": "run-8f3a2c",
  "workflow": "renewal-risk-summary",
  "agent": "renewal-agent",
  "principalArn": "arn:aws:sts::123456789012:assumed-role/BedrockRuntimeRole/gw-alex",
  "team": "sales-ai",
  "costCenter": "CC-2041",
  "experiment": {
    "variant": "treatment",
    "holdout": False,
    "promptVersion": "v14",
    "policyVersion": "2026-07"
  },
  "ops": {
    "latencyMs": 41200,
    "retries": 1,
    "toolCalls": 6,
    "humanApprovals": 1,
    "humanMinutes": 35,
    "escalations": 0
  },
  "econ": {
    "inputTokens": 48210,
    "outputTokens": 3105,
    "cacheReadTokens": 31500,
    "estCostUsd": 0.87
  },
  "outcome": {
    "status": "success",
    "accepted": True,
    "reopened": False,
    "revenueEventId": "opp-44121"
  }
}

Three fields deserve emphasis:

experiment block: Stamped at run creation and propagated into Bedrock request metadata, so model-level and workflow-level records join cleanly.

humanMinutes: What most teams omit and most need. Without it, “the agent did the work” silently excludes the 35 minutes a human spent reviewing it.

revenueEventId: The hook that makes revenue attribution possible later. It costs nothing to record and can’t be reconstructed afterward.

The rule: If the workflow telemetry can’t answer the business question, the instrumentation is incomplete.

Join cost to outcomes

With invocation logs landing in Amazon S3 (Part 1) and workflow-run records in your analytics store, one join produces the metrics that matter. Amazon Bedrock logs record tokens, not dollars, so first build a view that prices each invocation from token counts and your model rate sheet, aggregated by run ID. Then query with Amazon Athena:

SELECT
  w.workflow,
  w.variant,
  COUNT(*) AS runs,
  SUM(IF(w.outcome_status = 'success', 1, 0)) AS successes,
  ROUND(SUM(c.est_cost_usd) /
    NULLIF(SUM(IF(w.outcome_status = 'success', 1, 0)), 0), 2)
    AS cost_per_success,
  ROUND(SUM(w.retries) * 1.0 /
    NULLIF(SUM(IF(w.outcome_status = 'success', 1, 0)), 0), 2)
    AS retries_per_success,
  ROUND(SUM(w.human_minutes) /
    NULLIF(SUM(IF(w.outcome_status = 'success', 1, 0)), 0), 1)
    AS human_min_per_success
FROM workflow_runs w
JOIN invocation_costs_by_run c ON c.run_id = w.run_id
GROUP BY w.workflow, w.variant
ORDER BY cost_per_success DESC
Note: Column names and join keys shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema and workflow telemetry store, which might vary by implementation.

Cost per successful outcome, retries per success, and human minutes per success are the three numbers that survive contact with a skeptical CFO. Cost per call flatters agents that loop. Cost per success doesn’t. Note the variant grouping: the same query, split by experiment arm, is the ROI comparison.

Compare agents and humans correctly

The most credible evaluation is an A/B or holdout test. Controlled treatment and control groups compare the agent-assisted workflow against the human baseline without confusing the result with market, seasonal, or organizational changes.

For customer-facing or revenue-linked workflows, randomize at the visitor, lead, account, or case level. For internal workflows (support operations, coding assistants), use matched cohorts: teams, repository groups, or pods.

The comparison covers four dimensions:

Efficiency: time to completion, hours recovered, queue-time reduction.

Quality: error rate, approval rate, reopen rate, escalation rate.

Cost: cost per task, cost per successful outcome, total cost to serve.

Business value: conversion lift, retention lift, expansion rate, revenue per rep or per workflow.

If the agent improves one dimension while meaningfully degrading another, the result is ambiguous and the deployment needs tuning.

Revenue: The hardest metric

Efficiency gains are the easiest part of the ROI story to prove. Revenue impact is harder, and it is the metric leadership funds against. In revenue-adjacent workflows, measure whether the agent improves conversion, time-to-response, deal progression, or revenue per rep. Holdout tests are the most reliable way to separate incremental revenue attributable to the agent from general business momentum.

When revenue lift is real, the conversation changes. The organization stops asking whether the Bedrock bill went up and starts asking whether the additional spend is buying a meaningful increase in business output.

The scorecard

Based on what we have observed working with customers, a strong operating model doesn’t require fifty metrics. What works is a small scorecard tied to decisions, reviewed on a regular cadence for every production agent.

The following thresholds are starting points, not prescriptions. Calibrate them against your own fleet data and organizational context.

DimensionMetricGreenYellowRed
AdoptionActive users / intended users>70%40-70%<40%
QualityTasks completed without rework>90%75-90%<75%
EfficiencyHours recovered per week>target50-100% of target<50% of target
CostCost per successful outcome≤budget1-1.5x budget>1.5x budget
Business impactKPI lift compared to baselineSignificantMarginalNone or negative

Green means scale: the agent beats baseline while meeting cost and quality thresholds. Yellow means tune: promising but needs work. Red means retire or redesign: the agent consumes cost without enough measurable value. The willingness to actually retire a red agent is what makes the rest of the scorecard credible.

Conclusion

In this post, you learned how to calculate the true cost of a model by accounting for four hidden cost drivers (tokenizer efficiency, output alignment, agentic loop efficiency, and reasoning overhead), how to reduce cost per task through prompt caching, model routing, output constraints, and batch inference, and how to prove agent ROI by measuring human baselines, instrumenting workflows as experiments, joining cost to outcomes, and running holdout comparisons.

The cost optimization half answers “why is this expensive and how do I fix it.” The ROI half answers “is the agent better than the humans were.” Together with Part 1’s operating model (attribute, observe, enforce, optimize, operate), they form a complete framework: you can see who spent it, explain why, reduce the waste, and justify what remains.

To get started, benchmark your top model candidates against your own prompts using Amazon Bedrock model evaluation, capture tokens and turns from the usage block or your invocation logs, price them against current Bedrock pricing, and divide by success rate. For ROI measurement, consult the Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens for agent cost governance best practices.

If you have found other techniques for reducing cost per task or measuring agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock, let us know in the comments.

About the authors

item.title: Building a self-service LLM gateway with Amazon Bedrock and…
item.description: Full title: Building a self-service LLM gateway with Amazon Bedrock and LiteLLM
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Building a self-service LLM gateway with Amazon Bedrock and LiteLLM

Developers want AI coding assistants with minimal setup. With a large language model (LLM) gateway and LiteLLM, they can quickly access foundation models (FMs) available on Amazon Bedrock while you gain visibility and usage control. Platform teams need to monitor latency and errors, finance teams need to attribute inference costs to teams and projects, and security teams need consistent access controls. An LLM gateway can help address these needs by providing a centrally managed access point to the models that power coding assistants.

In this post, we show how to build a self-service LLM gateway using Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles with LiteLLM running on AWS Fargate to abstract Amazon Bedrock behind an OpenAI-compatible API. With this pattern, developers can access foundation models through a single API with a dedicated key while you gain per-user cost controls and model performance observability. By the end, you will understand the pattern well enough to build your own version from the illustrative snippets and AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) constructs. This post uses Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku models for example purposes. For a list of models and availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

This LLM gateway pattern follows a straightforward request flow from the developer, through the LiteLLM layer, to Amazon Bedrock and the underlying FM. The following diagram illustrates the production topology behind that flow. For simplicity, we don’t cover the addition of Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, such as content filtering and grounding, but you would normally include appropriate responsible AI controls before deploying to production.

A developer’s OpenAI-compatible client reaches the LLM gateway through Amazon Route 53, Amazon CloudFront, and an Application Load Balancer (ALB). It authenticates to LiteLLM on Fargate with a per-user API key. Behind that, the request draws on Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) (PostgreSQL) for virtual-key and spend state. It also interacts with Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey as a cache, and AWS Secrets Manager for secrets. LiteLLM then ultimately invokes Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles using a scoped AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) task role. Amazon CloudWatch captures requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM) metrics and the quota alarm.

Figure 1: LLM gateway architecture (production topology)

The architecture consists of these core components:

  • LiteLLM on AWS Fargate: LiteLLM provides a proxy that exposes an OpenAI-compatible API. We run it on an AWS Fargate task with target-tracking Auto Scaling on CPU utilization. Developers point their tools at this endpoint and don’t interact with Amazon Bedrock directly.
  • Self-service portal: LiteLLM includes a lightweight portal for admin and developer self-service. This web app can integrate with your corporate single sign-on (SSO). Using the portal, operations engineers set the spend policy while developers self-provision API keys within those parameters.
  • Persistent and cache storage: LiteLLM uses Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey for non-persistent response caching. It also coordinates rate-limiting across AWS Fargate tasks. A separate Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL) database is the database of record for persistent state such as API key metadata and spend tracking.
  • Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles: Each model (such as Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku) gets its own inference profile, which you manage using the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). With this, you get per-model quota isolation and a clean abstraction layer between LiteLLM’s configuration and the model versioning of Amazon Bedrock.
  • Langfuse: Open source LLM observability for prompt-level telemetry, latency tracking, and debugging. It complements the infrastructure-level metrics of Amazon CloudWatch with application-level insight.

By using an OpenAI-compatible protocol, developers can configure their tools, such as Claude Code, Continue, and Cursor, with a single base URL and API key. Developers then operate at a level above the Amazon Bedrock backend and can swap models, add fallbacks, or migrate model providers without touching developer configurations.

Prerequisites

You will need an AWS account, Amazon Bedrock model access, and appropriate IAM permissions to deploy this project. You will also need LiteLLM. The LiteLLM AI Gateway component is open source and suitable for a small pilot with some limitations. LiteLLM documents the AI Gateway as free for up to five users with a license required beyond that. LiteLLM Enterprise is a scalable, production-minded licensed version that includes the open source gateway plus single sign-on, audit logs, delegated admin roles, and support. While the free tier supports virtual keys, the self-service key issuance described in this post requires the Enterprise version.

End-to-end configuration: Left to right

We walk through each configuration layer from the developer’s machine to the foundation model.

Step 1: Developer IDE configuration (for example, Claude Code)

Developers configure their coding assistant to point to the LLM gateway. This is the only configuration a developer needs to make to their tool:

{
  "apiProvider": "openai-compatible",
  "apiBaseUrl": "https://llm-gateway.internal.example.com/v1",
  "apiKey": "sk-user-abc123",
  "model": "claude-sonnet-4-20250514"
}

With that configuration, each developer gets their own API key from the self-service portal and drops it into their tool configuration.

Step 2: LiteLLM gateway configuration

Deploy LiteLLM to a container service following the LiteLLM documentation. In this example we are using AWS Fargate. This will include the portal, which you can open at http://localhost:4000/ui during local testing.

The LiteLLM gateway is where you will map and enforce model names to Amazon Bedrock inference profile ARNs with per-key spend limits:

model_list:
  - model_name: claude-sonnet-4-20250514
    litellm_params:
      model: bedrock/arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1:111122223333:application-inference-profile/sonnet-profile-id
      aws_region_name: us-east-1
      max_retries: 3
      timeout: 900  # 15 min for extended thinking
    # REQUIRED for spend tracking: when `model` is a raw inference-profile ARN,
    # LiteLLM can't find it in its built-in cost map and defaults the cost to $0
    # which means per-key `spend` stays 0 and budgets NEVER enforce. Set the
    # per-token costs explicitly.
    model_info:
      input_cost_per_token: 0.000003        # example cost
      output_cost_per_token: 0.000015    # example cost

  - model_name: claude-haiku-4-5
    litellm_params:
      model: bedrock/arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1:111122223333:application-inference-profile/haiku-profile-id
      aws_region_name: us-east-1
      timeout: 120
    model_info:
      input_cost_per_token: 0.000001       # example cost
      output_cost_per_token: 0.000005    # example cost

litellm_settings:
  max_budget: 250            # example per key cost
  budget_duration: 7d      # Rolling 7-day window
  max_parallel_requests: 10
  set_verbose: false
  cache: true
  cache_params:
    type: redis    # Valkey is protocol-compatible, so this stays "redis"
    host: elasticache-endpoint
    port: 6379
master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY
database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL

Set on the Fargate task from AWS Secrets Manager:

LITELLM_MASTER_KEY=sk-platform-admin-... DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:password@rds-endpoint:5432/litellm

Note: Don’t hardcode the master_key or database credentials in config.yaml. LiteLLM resolves os.environ/VAR_NAME references at load time, so set LITELLM_MASTER_KEY and DATABASE_URL as environment variables on the Fargate task, sourced from AWS Secrets Manager. Set the Langfuse credentials the same way in Step 5.

When a developer calls claude-sonnet-4-20250514, for example, LiteLLM resolves it to the inference profile ARN. It then authenticates to Amazon Bedrock using the AWS Fargate task’s IAM role and streams the response back in OpenAI format.

Step 3: Bedrock inference profiles (CDK)

With Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles you can create named endpoints for specific models, so you get quota isolation and fine-grained IAM control.

Choosing cross-Region inference (CRIS): Geographic or Global

Amazon Bedrock CRIS avoids the overhead of implementing cross-Region request routing yourself. Other benefits include:

  • Access to a broader pool of Regional capacity.
  • Automatic routing of requests to a supported Region with available capacity.
  • Broader model selection, because some models are available only through an inference profile.

For this proxy pattern, we recommend Global cross-Region inference when the selected models support it and organizational policies permit inference processing across supported AWS commercial Regions worldwide. Geographic cross-Region inference keeps processing within a defined geography. For example, a US inference profile routes requests only to supported US Regions. Global cross-Region inference provides access to a broader pool of Regional capacity with potential pricing benefits compared with Geographic cross-Region inference. You can verify model availability, applicable service quotas, and model-specific pricing through current AWS documentation and AWS pricing pages.

CDK construct

import * as cdk from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import * as bedrock from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-bedrock';
import * as iam from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-iam';

// Create an Application Inference Profile pointing to the Global CRIS
// system-defined inference profile (note the `global.` prefix in the ARN).
const sonnetProfile = new bedrock.CfnApplicationInferenceProfile(this, 'SonnetProfile', {
  inferenceProfileName: 'claude-sonnet-gateway',
  modelSource: {
    copyFrom: `arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1:${this.account}:inference-profile/global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-20250514-v1:0`,
  },
  description: 'Claude Sonnet for developer coding assistants (Global CRIS)',
});

// Grant LiteLLM's task role access to invoke the profile.
// For Global CRIS, include the inference profile, the regional FM, and the global FM resources.
litellmTaskRole.addToPolicy(new iam.PolicyStatement({
  effect: iam.Effect.ALLOW,
  actions: ['bedrock:InvokeModel', 'bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream'],
  resources: [
    sonnetProfile.attrInferenceProfileArn,
    'arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1::foundation-model/anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-20250514-v1:0',
    'arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-20250514-v1:0',
  ],
}));

Important: For Global CRIS, the copyFrom ARN must reference the system-defined inference profile prefixed with global., not the foundation-model ARN directly. Using a foundation-model ARN creates a single-Region profile without cross-Region routing. Additionally, the IAM policy must include the resource ARNs the invocation actually touches: the application inference profile and the underlying foundation model in any Region it might route to (Region-wildcarded). Scoping only to the application-inference-profile ARN returns not authorized to perform: bedrock:InvokeModel on resource: arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1::foundation-model/... at invoke time. This is scoped least-privilege: it names the exact models in use, not bedrock: or .

Step 4: Bedrock invokes the foundation model

The inference profile handles model resolution and cross-Region routing transparently without additional configuration. When LiteLLM calls the inference profile ARN, Amazon Bedrock routes to available capacity across configured AWS Regions and returns the response.

Step 5: Langfuse observability

LiteLLM integrates with Langfuse through logging callbacks, providing visibility into model invocations without requiring changes to developer tool configurations. To enable the integration, merge the following entries into the existing litellm_settings block from the Step 2 configuration, preserving existing callback entries:

litellm_settings:
  success_callback: ["langfuse"]
  failure_callback: ["langfuse"]  # also log failed requests

Configure the Langfuse public key, secret key, and deployment endpoint as environment variables on the Fargate task. Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager:

LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY=pk-lf-...
LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY=sk-lf-...
LANGFUSE_HOST=https://us.cloud.langfuse.com  # or your self-hosted URL

The endpoint must match the selected Langfuse Cloud region or self-hosted deployment. Choose the hosting option based on data governance and operational requirements. Before enabling prompt and response logging, review the content captured by the integration and configure appropriate redaction, retention, and access controls.

Langfuse traces can include prompts, responses, model parameters, token usage, and latency, depending on the integration and logging configuration. This information helps investigate unexpected model responses and complements the operational metrics collected in Amazon CloudWatch.

Implementing cost controls

Cost controls are an important dimension to a successful AI strategy. Without cost controls, heavy usage of extended thinking features can lead to unexpectedly high charges, which we observed in our early pilots.

The spend limits configured in Step 2 (max_budget: 250, budget_duration: 7d) enforce a rolling 7-day window per API key, provided per-model model_info costs are set (refer to the Step 2 note). When a user reaches their limit, LiteLLM returns an HTTP 429 code with a clear message explaining that their budget has been exceeded. There’s no silent degradation or surprise bill. Developers and engineering teams can check current spend and reset timing through any of the following:

  • Daily spend: Query GET /user/daily/activity with a start_date and end_date range to get per-day metrics: spend, prompt tokens, completion tokens, and API requests, broken down by model, provider, and API key.
  • Per user spend: Query GET /user/info?user_id=… for a summary of a user’s total spend and the spend on each of their associated API keys.
  • Portal dashboard: The Admin UI (at https://<proxy-host>/ui) includes a Usage tab where developers and admins can browse spend by model, user, and tag without hitting the API directly.

These same endpoints are how your finance team gets per-user attribution without you building custom metering infrastructure. A scheduled job hitting /user/daily/activity or /global/spend/report is enough to feed a cost dashboard or chargeback report.

Developer self-service portal

The self-service portal also handles key lifecycle processes. Developers authenticate with your corporate SSO to generate a key bound to their identity, which they can later regenerate if the key is exposed or to match a rotation policy. Platform engineers configure the budget policy once for individual developers to autonomously operate within their constraints. Two things developers use the portal for directly:

  • Key generation: On the Admin UI’s Virtual Keys page (https://<proxy-host>/ui), developers authenticated through SSO choose Generate Key to create their own key, bound to their identity.
  • Rate limit visibility: Each /chat/completions response includes x-litellm-key-remaining-requests-{model} and x-litellm-key-remaining-tokens-{model} headers, so developers can see their remaining RPM and TPM headroom for that model directly in their tool’s response. This is distinct from the dollar-based spend tracking earlier in this post.

Monitoring and observability

For an LLM gateway, traditional metrics like latency percentiles can be misleading, especially with extended thinking models, where a single request can take several minutes. Instead, we focus on requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM) as primary signals. Here, Amazon CloudWatch can help you monitor and alarm for these signals with the following configuration.

Amazon CloudWatch alarms for quota management

new cloudwatch.Alarm(this, 'BedrockTPMAlarm', {
  metric: new cloudwatch.Metric({
    namespace: 'LiteLLM/Gateway',
    metricName: 'TokensPerMinute',
    statistic: 'Sum',
    period: cdk.Duration.minutes(1),
  }),
  // Alert at ~60% of your account's TPM quota (check Service Quotas for your
  // actual limit, defaults vary by model and account).
  threshold: 600000,
  evaluationPeriods: 3,
  comparisonOperator: cloudwatch.ComparisonOperator.GREATER_THAN_THRESHOLD,
  alarmDescription: 'TPM approaching Bedrock quota - request increase proactively',
});

Note that the alarm configuration alerts at 60–70 percent quota utilization rather than waiting for throttling. This provides lead time to scale Amazon Bedrock quotas before users experience degradation.

Emitting the metric: LiteLLM has no built-in callback that publishes a metric named TokensPerMinute to a LiteLLM/Gateway namespace, so the alarm needs a source. A small custom-logger callback that calls CloudWatch PutMetricData on each request does the job. Register it through litellm_settings.success_callback (which is additive), not callbacks. The callbacks list replaces LiteLLM’s internal logger list, which includes the built-in spend-tracking logger, and will silently disable budget enforcement.

Here’s a minimal version of that callback, using LiteLLM’s CustomLogger class:

import boto3
from litellm.integrations.custom_logger import CustomLogger

cloudwatch = boto3.client("cloudwatch")

class TPMEmitter(CustomLogger):
    async def async_log_success_event(self, kwargs, response_obj, start_time, end_time):
        total_tokens = kwargs.get("standard_logging_object", {}).get("total_tokens", 0)
        cloudwatch.put_metric_data(
            Namespace="LiteLLM/Gateway",
            MetricData=[{
                "MetricName": "TokensPerMinute",
                "Value": total_tokens,
                "Unit": "Count",
            }],
        )

# Register alongside success_callback, not in place of it:
import litellm
litellm.callbacks = [TPMEmitter()]

For prompt-level debugging, we run Langfuse alongside CloudWatch. When a developer reports “the model gave a bad response,” you can use Langfuse to inspect the exact prompt, token counts, and model parameters. For compliance-sensitive environments, Amazon Bedrock’s native invocation logging to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) provides an immutable audit trail.

Lessons learned at scale

We deployed this pattern end-to-end on a fresh AWS account to confirm the sample snippets work. In our own deployment, we scaled this LLM gateway to several hundred developers and learned several lessons.

Operational lessons

The main findings from running at scale:

  • Extended thinking changes everything about latency. Requests using Claude’s extended thinking can take several minutes or longer, depending on the thinking budget. If your load balancer has a 60-second idle timeout, those requests will fail silently. To address that, you can set load balancer idle timeouts to at least 900 seconds and configure LiteLLM’s request timeout accordingly (timeout: 900 in the Step 2 configuration earlier in this post).
  • When throttled, back off and retry on the same model before initiating a fallback. Our initial instinct was to fall back from Sonnet to Haiku upon throttling. But this is suboptimal for coding assistants because changing models breaks the consistent behavior developers rely on. Instead, retry the same model with exponential backoff at the proxy level (max_retries: 3 in Step 2). When a request cannot be served after retries, surface the error clearly rather than returning an alternate model’s completions.
  • Separate automation tool invocations from developer traffic. continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines and automated code review tools should call Amazon Bedrock directly with their own inference profiles and quotas. Mixing automation traffic with interactive developer traffic leads to unpredictable latency and hinders meaningful cost attribution.
  • Start with Global CRIS from day one, if feasible. We initially used Geographic (US) CRIS but ultimately migrated our inference profiles when we reached Regional quota limits. For our use case, we didn’t have data residency constraints so we could use Global CRIS. Global CRIS routes requests across Regions to draw on a broader capacity pool, simplifying management at scale.

Deployment considerations

Two configuration mistakes are common and hard to notice until spend or connectivity breaks:

Configuring per-model costs is mandatory for enforcing budgets. The model_info block on each model isn’t optional if you want to track per-user cost controls. When model points at an Amazon Bedrock inference-profile ARN, LiteLLM can’t look up the ARN in its built-in pricing table. It instead records $0 per token, so the max_budget and 429 throttle enforcement silently don’t trigger. Spend remains at $0 no matter how many tokens flow. Fix this by setting input_cost_per_token and output_cost_per_token (or input_cost_per_million_tokens).

Database compared to cache: The database_url must be PostgreSQL. LiteLLM’s virtual keys (/key/generate), store_model_in_db, and spend tracking are Postgres-backed.

A handful of smaller deployment details rounded out our checklist:

  • Global CRIS IAM needs the foundation-model resources, not only the app-inference-profile ARN. Otherwise, invocation is denied at runtime.
  • Give the Fargate task enough memory. LiteLLM’s gateway image runs out of memory and is killed at 512 MB (exit 137) before it can pass a health check. About 2 GB is a safe floor.
  • Override the container entryPoint. The official image’s entrypoint is litellm. If you render a config at startup with a shell script, set entryPoint: ['/bin/sh','-c'] or your script is passed as arguments to litellm.
  • IAM role and security-group descriptions must be ASCII. Em-dashes and -> arrows are rejected by IAM and Amazon EC2.
  • Confirm model availability in your account and Region. Model IDs and CRIS profiles change. Verify with aws bedrock list-inference-profiles (for example, we used claude-haiku-4-5 because claude-haiku-3-5 was not available).

Clean up

This post walks through the pattern with illustrative snippets rather than a single deployable stack, there’s no one-command teardown. But the architecture relies on several resources that continue to bill while they run. These include the AWS Fargate service, Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL), Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey, and the Application Load Balancer, along with supporting Secrets Manager secrets, CloudWatch alarms, and Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles. When you finish testing, remove them to avoid ongoing charges.

If you deployed the full solution using the Guidance for Multi-Provider Generative AI Gateway on AWS, follow that solution’s cleanup instructions to remove everything it created. For AWS CDK, run cdk destroy. For AWS CloudFormation, delete the stack.

If you built the pattern yourself from the snippets in this post, remove each resource:

  • AWS Fargate service and cluster: Delete the Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) service to stop and drain the tasks, then delete the cluster.
  • Application Load Balancer: Delete the ALB along with its listeners and target groups.
  • Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL): Delete the database instance. Take a final snapshot first only if you need to retain API key and spend data.
  • Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey: Delete the replication group or cluster. It holds only cache data, so no snapshot is needed.
  • Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles: Delete the profiles created in Step 3, either by removing the AWS CDK construct or by running aws bedrock delete-inference-profile.
  • AWS Secrets Manager secrets: Schedule deletion of the proxy’s secrets, such as the master key and database credentials.
  • Amazon CloudWatch alarms and log groups: Delete the TPM alarm and any LiteLLM log groups.

Delete the AWS Fargate service and ALB before the Amazon RDS and ElastiCache endpoints they depend on, so running tasks don’t error against removed backends during teardown.

Conclusion

In this post, we detailed a pattern for an LLM gateway that abstracts the multi-model architecture of Amazon Bedrock to provide your teams with scalable and observable self-service access. Because Amazon Bedrock routes across models through a single interface without changing infrastructure, your developers get instant access to foundation models through familiar APIs. Cost governance, observability, and a single control plane go to your engineering and security teams while finance gets per-user attribution without you building a custom metering infrastructure.

Start by working through the pattern and snippets in this post to understand how the pieces fit together. The AWS CDK snippets cover the Amazon Bedrock application inference profile, its IAM policy, and the CloudWatch alarm. The surrounding AWS Fargate service, Amazon RDS, Amazon ElastiCache, ALB, and AWS Secrets Manager resources follow standard AWS CDK patterns and aren’t shown.

When you’re ready for a complete, deployable implementation, the Guidance for Multi-Provider Generative AI Gateway on AWS closely aligns with this pattern. You can find the guide on the AWS Solutions Library with the accompanying blog post and GitHub projects. While this post stepped through the same core pattern, it focused on Amazon Bedrock for developer coding assistants. The larger solution architecture adds multi-provider support, Amazon ECS or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon CloudFront and AWS WAF options, and an admin UI.

Explore the components of this architecture with additional documentation for Amazon Bedrock Inference Profiles, LiteLLM gateway, AWS Fargate, and Langfuse.

Try this pattern in your organization. Start with a pilot team, validate the cost controls, and scale from there.

About the authors

item.title: Run agents securely and efficiently with the next generation…
item.description: Full title: Run agents securely and efficiently with the next generation AgentCore runtime
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Run agents securely and efficiently with the next generation AgentCore runtime

AI agents have moved past one-off prompts. They now run multi-step workloads for hours at a time. The length of task that frontier agents can complete on their own doubles about every four months (METR), and 40 percent of large enterprises are scaling AI agents, up from 27 percent a year ago (McKinsey). As agents run longer and with more autonomy, the focus shifts from what agents can do to how securely, reliably, and economically they can operate at scale. Agents do more than traditional software: they execute code, navigate browsers, access sensitive data, and act on behalf of users. These capabilities introduce new security and infrastructure demands, making strong isolation essential for production deployments.

Every agent session needs a secure, isolated environment. But delivering that isolation at scale introduces a fundamental challenge: balancing performance, cost, and efficiency. Pre-provisioned environments consume resources even when idle, driving up costs. On-demand environments reduce wasted capacity but introduce cold-start latency, delaying agent execution. Neither approach scales efficiently without trade-offs. As organizations move from deploying a handful of agents to running thousands of concurrent sessions, building and managing custom sandboxes becomes increasingly complex, expensive, and unpredictable.

The challenge is evident. Only 15 percent of organizations have scaled orchestrated, multi-agent systems, and 70 percent say they can’t yet trust and govern their agents (Deloitte). Scaling agents shouldn’t mean choosing between security, speed, and cost. The next generation of agent infrastructure must deliver strong isolation with fast startup times, elastic scaling, and usage-based economics. Because as AI agents move into production, secure execution shouldn’t be the bottleneck. It should be the foundation that makes scale possible. The fastest path to production should also be the safest one.

The next generation AgentCore runtime

We built Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to help developers build, connect, and optimize agents securely at scale. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is the managed compute layer. It gives developers a fully managed environment to deploy and run agents without building or maintaining infrastructure. Since launching, our customers have been pushing their agents into increasingly complex workloads. As those workloads grow, so do the demands on the execution environment: more compute, more flexible billing, and trust boundaries that extend to data, not only compute. Agents reach production at scale if the infrastructure underneath was built for both scale and speed.

Today we’re announcing updates to AgentCore runtime that meet those demands. The core guarantee stands: every session runs in its own hardware-isolated Firecracker micro virtual machine (MicroVM), with its own identity, policy, and audit trail. These updates expand what’s possible within that guarantee. Sessions now start up to 15x faster, scale to 4x more compute, and run up to 68% more efficiently, with the isolation boundary fully intact.

Here’s what’s new.

Run bigger workloads without waiting longer to start

Teams building increasingly advanced agents asked for more flexibility: the ability to scale memory and compute within the isolated session to match the demands of their workloads. From large codebase compilations to browser-driven workflows to local model inference, the execution environment needs to keep pace.

Sessions now scale 4x compared to the previous version, up to 8 vCPUs and 32 GB, with support for container images up to 10 GB. Sessions start in under 2 seconds, independent of image size and concurrency. You no longer need warm pools and pre-provisioned clusters to manage cold starts.

“AgentCore Runtime lets us run AI-driven development at scale. Each coding agent session runs in its own hardware-isolated environment, which we need when agents execute code, and the runtime scales elastically with demand and starts fast every time, so our engineers move quickly without managing any infrastructure.”
— Siwei Shen, VP of Engineering, Coinbase
“Mission is using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime to power a natural-language query agent that helps users retrieve property and sales insights without navigating complex data systems. In our initial comparison of both runtime versions, the same workload delivered 35% faster cold starts for inference requests and 77% faster starts for health checks, while reducing measured runtime cost per call by 17%. The new AgentCore runtime gives us a compelling combination of faster agent experiences and more efficient resource utilization as we bring enterprise agents into production.”
— Dr. Ryan Ries, Chief AI & Data Scientist, Mission Cloud
“Our approach is to run Zuora’s cloud with automation and AI agents wherever we can, and that only works if the runtime is efficient and reliable. The next generation AgentCore runtime cut our memory footprint per invocation by around 60% in many use cases while handling more traffic at steady latency. That gives us a stronger cost profile as we expand agentic workloads across our platform.”
— Brad Ruppert, VP of Cloud and Security, Zuora
“The Rescale platform helps R&D and engineering teams accelerate product development with agentic digital engineering. Our engineering-specific agents validate simulation inputs, troubleshoot jobs, select hardware, and generate reports, while engineers stay in control. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime allows us to deploy and scale those agents in production without building or operating the underlying agent infrastructure, so we can deliver new agents to customers faster.”
— Mark Whitney, VP Engineering, Rescale

Stop paying for idle agents

As teams move agents closer to production, they asked for billing that reflects how agents actually work. Agents spend much of their time waiting on a model response, a tool call, or a human decision. Agents should be billed for the work they do, not the time they spend waiting.

The runtime now reclaims memory within minutes of the agent releasing it, and an idle agent scales to zero. For multi-turn agents with natural pauses between interactions, this means up to 68 percent less memory consumed per session. For always-on agents, committed baseline pricing sets a memory baseline per session, billed as a minimum, with room to burst up to four times that baseline on demand. This gives steady workloads a predictable rate at AWS Lambda MicroVM rates. The runtime uses compute more efficiently, so you pay less for the same work. That makes the finance conversation that often gates production rollouts easier to close.

“The next generation Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime helps us deliver more responsive AI experiences by starting agents faster and using memory more efficiently. Aligning consumption with actual usage gives our clients great confidence to scale agentic solutions while keeping costs connected to real demand.”
— Ashwin Patil, Principal, AI and Data Leader, Deloitte Consulting LLP
“AgentCore runtime gives us a managed foundation for building agentic products and platforms around our customers’ data, tools, and business processes. The next generation Agentcore runtime makes that foundation more responsive and resource-efficient by restoring initialized environments and reclaiming unused memory. We’re beginning to build on the latest version because the cost and latency reductions make a significant difference in how our customers’ businesses operate.”
— Randall Hunt, CTO, Caylent

Isolation now extends to your data

Many enterprises face a persistent gap in their agent security model. The agent runs inside an isolated session, but the data it requires resides outside that boundary. Long-running agents pick up context as they go: files, credentials, tool outputs, and more. Teams end up building their own rules for how data moves in and out, adding complexity and risk with every new agent.

Isolation that stops at compute is only half a boundary. The next generation AgentCore runtime closes that gap. Each session still runs in its own hardware-isolated environment with its own identity, access policy, and audit trail. Agents can now dynamically mount and save their work to a filesystem, such as an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket with FUSE support. Your data stays inside the trust boundary for the entire job, governed by a single set of controls you define once.

“At Okta, the combination of AgentCore runtime and Lambda MicroVMs provide the isolated execution environment and contextual memory our agents need to inspect code, run test suites, and open pull requests within ephemeral sandboxes. Paired with our identity-governed policy controls, AgentCore Runtime and Lambda MicroVMs demonstrate how we can safely scale autonomous engineering agents without risking workspace leakage or privilege escalation.”
— Monica Bajaj, SVP Engineering, Okta
“From helping car shoppers value a trade-in to helping dealers book service appointments and structure deals, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore powers dozens of agentic solutions across Cox Automotive’s brands. Having a single, governed agent platform lets our teams across our business move from pilot to production with confidence.”
— Chris Dillon, VP, Product and Engineering, Cox Automotive
“With the next generation of CoCounsel Legal, we set out to build an agentic system that does more than answer questions: it works through a matter end to end, from research to trusted work product. Getting that into customers’ hands quickly meant spending our time on legal reasoning and quality, rather than on running agent infrastructure. With AgentCore Runtime handling the hosting and scaling, we moved from prototype to production fast and kept complete control over how our agents operate and integrate with our existing systems. Our developers build on their preferred frameworks, and Runtime gives us the enterprise-grade reliability and isolation we need to run CoCounsel’s agentic legal workflows at scale for legal professionals around the world.”
— Danilo Tommasina, Distinguished Engineer – Thomson Reuters

Our commitment

The agents that reach production are the ones you trust to act on your behalf, with real data, real stakes, and real accountability. Trust isn’t a feature you add later. It’s the runtime you build on. This release is a step toward that future: bigger sessions, efficient resource use, and storage inside the trust boundary, without loosening the isolation that makes the work trustworthy. By re:Invent, per-session scoping will bind each session to its own storage folder through session-labeled credentials, and we will keep building from there.

Get started

The next generation AgentCore runtime is available today in AWS Regions across North America, South America, Europe, and Asia Pacific. Visit Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to build on it or open the Amazon Bedrock console to start exploring.

About the author

item.title: Migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with your c…
item.description: Full title: Migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with your coding agent
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with your coding agent

With a customer-managed knowledge base on Amazon Bedrock, you provision and scale the vector store, tune the embedding model and index settings, and plan capacity for each new data source. The migration guide in the Agent Toolkit for AWS helps you migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base. Managed Knowledge Base takes over that work and adds new retrieval capabilities, and your team keeps control of the content and the application that uses it.

Moving a production knowledge base means your team maps its configuration, creates the replacement, ingests content, updates the application’s retrieval call, and validates retrieval before switching traffic. To help, we added a knowledge base migration guide to the amazon-bedrock skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS. The guide gives your coding agent the context to plan the migration with you, starting with read-only discovery and a plan you review line by line. On your approval, the agent creates the new knowledge base and its data sources alongside the original, or writes a migrated infrastructure as code (IaC) template for your pipeline. Ingestion and updating your application’s Retrieve calls stay with you, and your agent can walk you through both.

In this post, we explain why we recommend the move and how the migration guide works, review the prerequisites, install the skill, plan a migration, update the application’s retrieval call, and validate retrieval before cutover.

Why move to Managed Knowledge Base

We recommend Managed Knowledge Base because it balances ease of use, retrieval accuracy, and cost.

AWS runs the store

With a Managed Knowledge Base, Amazon Bedrock handles ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval, and the store scales automatically as your content grows. Hybrid search, which combines keyword and semantic matching, is always on, with no index to configure. The knowledge base includes a managed embedding model, a managed reranker, and a built-in parser for multimodal file types.

You can still bring your own Amazon Bedrock embedding model when you create the knowledge base. On each retrieval request, you choose the managed reranker, an Amazon Bedrock reranking model, or no reranking. The managed reranker requires the managed embedding model.

Built-in capabilities

Managed Knowledge Base includes capabilities you’d otherwise build yourself:

  • Native connectors ingest content directly from sources such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Microsoft SharePoint, and Atlassian Confluence. For the current list, see supported connectors. After the first full sync, later syncs pick up only changes, on demand or on a schedule. The Managed Knowledge Base includes a deletion safeguard to help protect against accidental bulk removal of indexed content.
  • Access control list (ACL) awareness ingests document permissions with the content, so retrieval returns only what the signed-in user can access. For connectors that support it, such as Microsoft SharePoint and Atlassian Confluence, a real-time check against the source also catches permission changes since the last sync. ACL awareness doesn’t authenticate users, so your application must verify and pass the user’s identity.
  • Agentic retrieval answers questions that a single search can’t by handling multi-part questions and retrieving iteratively. It can search more than one knowledge base in a single request.
  • Integration with AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, exposes your knowledge base as a target. Any client that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) can then query the knowledge base, and the gateway handles authentication.
  • Resource-based policies let applications in other AWS accounts use one team’s knowledge base. Scope each policy to the specific roles that call the knowledge base, and grant only the actions they use, such as bedrock:Retrieve.

Agentic retrieval, AgentCore Gateway integration, and resource-based policies are not available on customer-managed knowledge bases. For the AWS Regions where managed knowledge bases are available, and the features that AWS GovCloud (US-West) doesn’t support, see Supported AWS Regions.

Higher quotas

As of this writing, higher default quotas change how you can organize content. With 200 data sources per knowledge base, you can group related content in one knowledge base. With 10,000 knowledge bases per account, per Region, each team or product line can use a separate knowledge base.

Default quotaCustomer-managedManaged
Knowledge bases per account, per Region10010,000
Data sources per knowledge base5200
Concurrent ingestion jobs per knowledge base150
Query input characters1,00010,000

For current values, see Amazon Bedrock endpoints and quotas and Service quotas for managed knowledge bases.

Pay for what you store and retrieve

Cost is one of three things teams weigh when they consider this move, alongside customizability and direct control of the vector store. On a customer-managed knowledge base, you choose, provision, scale, and update the vector and text stores, and pay separately for the infrastructure you select. On a Managed Knowledge Base, those stages are part of the service, and storage and retrieval are metered directly.

The pricing models can differ too. With a customer-managed knowledge base, storage and retrieval charges depend on the vector store you choose. Some stores charge for provisioned or minimum capacity, and others, such as Amazon S3 Vectors, a capability of Amazon S3, charge only for what you use. A Managed Knowledge Base is priced on what you store and retrieve, so cost follows real usage. Usage-based pricing can fit enterprise question-answering, policy, and support knowledge bases that run at low utilization. For current rates, see Amazon Bedrock pricing. For the parsers available on a customer-managed knowledge base and how each is billed, see Parsing options for your data source.

Cost driverCustomer-managed knowledge baseManaged Knowledge Base
Vector storagePriced separately by your chosen store. A provisioned retrieval service can have a minimum idle cost even at low volumeIncluded in the base storage rate of $5 per GB per month
Multimodal document parsingRequires Amazon Bedrock Data Automation, billed by page or image, or a foundation model, billed by token. Text-only parsing is free.Included
Embedding generationBilled separately at your embedding model’s rateIncluded with the default model. Charges apply only if you choose a custom model
Ingestion, sync, and re-sync computeRe-embedding, orchestration code, and indexing compute spikes on each sync add recurring costIncluded, with incremental sync that processes only new and changed content
ConnectorsBuilding and running custom connectors can add compute costNative connectors are included
Standard retrievalNo Amazon Bedrock charge per query. Your vector store can charge per query, as Amazon S3 Vectors does.$1 per 1,000 retrieval requests
RerankingAmazon Rerank is charged at $1 per 1,000 queries. A custom reranking model is billed at its own rateIncluded in the $1 per 1,000 retrieval requests
Agentic retrievalYou build the agentic workflow on a Bedrock model, which can cost roughly $18 to $24 per 1,000 queries before development and maintenance. Because model usage is billed by token, the price per query varies.Agentic retrieval costs an additional $4 per 1,000 queries on top of the underlying retrieval calls, including multi-shot retrieval, reranking, and answer generation. Depending on the number of underlying retrieval calls, the total can range from roughly $6 to $9 per 1,000 queries.

Rates are only part of the total cost of ownership. On a customer-managed knowledge base, your team provisions, scales, and operates each stage as a separate resource. A Managed Knowledge Base consolidates them into one resource, with a default embedding model, foundation model, and reranker, and with per-knowledge-base rate limits by default. You manage the content and the application that uses it, and Amazon Bedrock operates the managed storage, embedding model, foundation model, and reranker.

Solution overview

A customer-managed knowledge base uses the VECTOR type, with a vector store you configure. A Managed Knowledge Base uses the MANAGED type. The migration guide directs your agent to create a new MANAGED knowledge base alongside the original without modifying or deleting the original during migration. Using the guide’s map, your agent writes a plan that lists which settings remain unchanged, which Managed handles differently, and which application changes you need to make. As Figure 1 shows, the original keeps serving every request while your team ingests content, validates, and cuts over.

Figure 1: Create a managed knowledge base or migrated template alongside the original, then validate before cutover

How the migration guide works

The guide separates planning from implementation. In Explore mode, your agent answers questions about Managed Knowledge Base and can inspect your configuration with read-only calls, so you can estimate the effort. In Migration mode, the guide takes your agent through checkpoints:

  • Introduce and choose. Your agent explains what it will and won’t touch. Choose the mode, a live knowledge base or IaC source, and a plain (default) or technical explanation style.
  • Identify. Confirm the account and AWS Region. Your agent flags over-broad credentials, asks whether you want a cost analysis, and creates an output directory.
  • Discover. Your agent reads the knowledge base and data sources with read-only calls, or reads your template files.
  • Plan. Review the plan and application changes. By default, your agent stops here.
  • Implement, if requested. For a live build, approve the exact preview of the provisioning script, and approve again if it changes. For IaC, your agent writes a migrated template and reports which schema checks ran.
  • Handoff. Review what was produced and your team’s remaining steps.

As Figure 2 shows, resource creation stays separate from ingestion and cutover.

Figure 2: Migration checkpoints. Implementation is optional, and your team runs ingestion and cutover

Review the configuration mapping

The guide maps each setting to preserve your data sources, filters, and chunking behavior when the managed type uses a different configuration. The plan classifies each setting:

  • 1:1. The new knowledge base uses the same setting.
  • Adjusted. Managed uses a different setting for the same outcome, and the plan applies the substitution.
  • Blocked. There is no managed path today. Your agent excludes that knowledge base from the build, explains why, and points you to AWS Support. Other knowledge bases in the same run can proceed.

Compare chunking on your own content when you validate.

Review the permissions and generated changes

Discovery, planning, and the entire IaC path need only read-only credentials. For a live build, the guide directs your agent to propose a scoped policy that explicitly denies changes to the original knowledge base, and to never ask for administrator or full-access permissions. It also directs your agent to change only resources it created, reference secrets by Amazon Resource Name (ARN), and ignore instructions found in the data it reads. Review the generated AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy and provisioning script before you approve the run. After the build, check what the agent did in AWS CloudTrail event history, which keeps 90 days of management events. Each event records the API call, such as CreateKnowledgeBase, and the identity that made it.

For the optional cost analysis, your agent compares current spend with a Managed Knowledge Base estimate using current AWS prices. It uses read-only inputs, including Amazon CloudWatch metrics, Amazon S3 object sizes, and AWS Cost Explorer. Each figure is labeled as measured, supplied by you, or estimated.

Prerequisites

Use separate credentials for planning and for any approved resource creation.

  • A compatible development environment with the Agent Toolkit for AWS.
  • The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), configured with a least-privilege, read-only profile.
  • Access to the original knowledge base configuration or its IaC files.
  • For the optional live build: A scoped build profile, using the policy the guide recommends. An IAM service role for the new knowledge base. The guide gives your agent the trust policy and permissions to help you create it. Python 3 with boto3 for the generated provisioning script.

The Agent Toolkit for AWS works with compatible development environments and its repository on GitHub lists the available skills. Examples in this post use AWS CLI 2.37 and boto3 1.43.32.

Install the skill

Follow the Agent Toolkit for AWS getting-started instructions for your coding agent. The add-skill command installs the amazon-bedrock skill to the coding agents it detects. Add --agent to target one, for example --agent kiro.

aws agent-toolkit add-skill \
    --skill-name amazon-bedrock

After installation, your agent loads the migration guide when you describe a migration task. The following prompts are illustrative inputs, not transcripts.

Plan the migration

Choose the path that matches how you maintain the source.

PathWhat your agent readsWhat it producesAWS changes
ExploreDocumentation, and optionally your knowledge base (read-only)Answers in the conversationNone
Live knowledge baseYour knowledge base and data sources (read-only)A plan, and optionally a new Managed Knowledge Base alongside the originalOnly after you approve the exact preview
Infrastructure as codeYour AWS CloudFormation template, AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) synthesized template, or Terraform configurationA migrated template in the same formatNone. Your pipeline deploys it

To start in Explore mode, ask a question:

What would change if I moved knowledge base <your-kb-name>
in <your-region> to a Managed Knowledge Base? Use Explore mode.

When you’re ready, choose the live or IaC path.

Migrate a live knowledge base

Ask for a plan before authorizing resource creation:

Plan a migration of knowledge base <your-kb-name> in <your-region>
to a Managed Knowledge Base. Stop after the plan.

Confirm the account and Region, then review the plan’s mappings and application changes. By default, the new knowledge base takes the original’s name with a -managed suffix. To build it, confirm the service role exists, switch to the build profile, inspect the provisioning script and its preview, and approve. Your agent runs the script, which creates the knowledge base and data sources, and reports their status.

Migrate infrastructure as code

Point your agent at the source template or configuration:

Review <path-to-source-template> and plan a migration to a
Managed Knowledge Base.

Your agent writes the migrated file to the output directory, deploys nothing, and shows you the diff. To keep the diff, ask your agent to save it. Run terraform init -backend=false and terraform validate before deployment. Your agent can walk you through both commands, but the guide leaves these checks to you because terraform init downloads the large AWS provider. Before you apply the deployment plan, check that it keeps the original resources you need for rollback.

Example conversation

The migration runs as a conversation. Before reading anything, your agent states its scope and asks how to proceed:

It never changes or deletes <your-kb-id>, never starts ingestion,
and never cuts your application over; every AWS change is shown to
you and approved first. Nothing has run against your KB yet.

1. Mode: Explore (read-only Q&A about Managed KBs and your KB, no
   plan or build) or Migration (run the phases: identify, discover,
   plan, and optionally build)?
2. Target type, if Migration: migrate the live KB <your-kb-id> (kb
   path, which can build a new Managed KB on approval), or migrate
   the Terraform/CloudFormation that defines it (iac path, which
   only emits a migrated file and provisions nothing)?
3. Explanation style: plain or technical. I'll use plain unless
   you say otherwise.

The plan summary shows each mapping, the caller changes, and the decisions you need to make:

Phase 3, Plan: written (plan.md)
- Mapping:
  - Vector store becomes auto-provisioned (adjusted, Yes).
  - SEMANTIC chunking is dropped for the managed default
    (adjusted, Partly).
  - Parsing becomes SMART_PARSING (adjusted, Yes).
  - The S3 prefix and metadata sidecars carry over 1:1.
- Changes for callers:
  - New KB id.
  - managedSearchConfiguration replaces vectorSearchConfiguration.
  - overrideSearchType: SEMANTIC can't be sent; search is hybrid.
Your input needed before this can go further.
- D1 embeddingModelType: MANAGED (recommended): keeps the managed
  reranker. CUSTOM Titan v2 1024/FLOAT32: turns off the managed
  reranker.
- D2 aclEnabled: recommend false, since the source has no ACLs.
  On S3 this can't be changed after create.
- Next step: stop with this plan (the default), or opt into Phase 4?

For a live build, your agent stops at a preview, and the approval command requires the plan’s hash:

If you approve, the command to run is the following. It is MUTATING:
  AWS_PROFILE=build-profile AWS_REGION=<your-region> \
    python3 provision_managed_kb.py --execute \
    --expect-plan-sha256 <plan-sha256>
--execute refuses to start unless it is given --expect-plan-sha256
and the hash matches.
What the preview would create:
- Knowledge base (CreateKnowledgeBase, MANAGED): support-docs-managed
- Data source (CreateDataSource, managed connector, deletion
  protection ENABLED/15): support-docs-s3-managed
The script never calls StartIngestionJob, Retrieve, Update*,
Delete*, or a standalone TagResource.

Example exchanges are lightly edited, with identifiers replaced.

Update the application’s retrieval call

Your application uses the same Retrieve operation for both types. The managed request targets the new knowledge base ID and replaces vectorSearchConfiguration with managedSearchConfiguration. Passing vectorSearchConfiguration to a managed knowledge base returns a validation error. Managed retrieval always uses hybrid search, so the managed request shape has no overrideSearchType field. Metadata filters keep the same syntax, except that managed knowledge bases don’t support the startsWith and stringContains operators. For the full syntax, see the Retrieve API reference.

The example assumes both knowledge bases contain the locale metadata used by the filter.

# Illustrative: the managed request shape was checked with boto3 1.43.32; adapt the IDs and filter to your knowledge base.
import boto3

client = boto3.client("bedrock-agent-runtime")
query = {"text": "How do I return an online order?"}
locale_filter = {"equals": {"key": "locale", "value": "en-US"}}

# Customer-managed (VECTOR) knowledge base.
original_response = client.retrieve(
    knowledgeBaseId="<original-kb-id>",
    retrievalQuery=query,
    retrievalConfiguration={
        "vectorSearchConfiguration": {
            "numberOfResults": 5,
            "overrideSearchType": "SEMANTIC",
            "filter": locale_filter,
        }
    },
)

# Managed target: different ID and search configuration.
managed_response = client.retrieve(
    knowledgeBaseId="<managed-kb-id>",
    retrievalQuery=query,
    retrievalConfiguration={
        "managedSearchConfiguration": {
            "numberOfResults": 5,
            "filter": locale_filter,
        }
    },
)

Validate retrieval and cut over

Evaluate the new knowledge base while the application still uses the original.

  • If using IaC, review and deploy the target configuration through your pipeline.
  • Sync each data source and review any failures. See Sync your data.
  • Grant your application’s runtime IAM role bedrock:Retrieve on the new knowledge base ARN, and keep its access to the original knowledge base so you can roll back.
  • Run representative queries against both knowledge bases with Retrieve, using that role. The two types use different score scales. Managed scores also depend on rerankingModelType, which defaults to MANAGED with the managed embedding model and to NONE with a custom one. Tune thresholds per mode, and hold the mode constant while comparing.
  • Test metadata filters and permission-aware retrieval where used, including content the signed-in user shouldn’t receive. On an ACL-enabled data source, requests without userContext.userId (the user’s email) return no results.
  • After acceptance, deploy the new knowledge base ID and request shape. Keep the original knowledge base, with current content, and application configuration through your rollback period.

For each query, check whether both return the same top document and how much results overlap. A short script can report pass or fail against criteria such as a matching top document on at least 90 percent of queries and no zero-result queries on the managed knowledge base. Tune that threshold for your workload. For other retrieval quality measures, such as context relevance and context coverage, see Use metrics to understand RAG system performance.

Watch for these differences when you compare results:

  • Normalize source locations before comparison. A customer-managed knowledge base can return s3://bucket/key in location.s3Location.uri, and a managed knowledge base can return an https:// URL. Compare by object key.
  • Compare the top result instead of assuming equal result counts. The two knowledge base types can return different numbers of results, and numberOfResults sets a maximum rather than a guarantee. Compare the top document, and review each query where it changes. For details, see Configure and customize queries for managed knowledge bases.
  • Map renamed system metadata keys. For example, replace x-amz-bedrock-kb-data-source-id with _data_source_id in comparison code. Your own metadata attributes keep their names. For details, see Configure and customize queries for managed knowledge bases.

Clean up

If you complete the migration, retire the original only after the rollback period and a dependency review. Keep the source documents and buckets the managed knowledge base ingests from, and storage that other workloads use. Clean up IaC-managed resources through their owning template.

If you end the evaluation instead, keep the original and delete what you created in this order:

  • Delete each managed data source and wait until it’s gone.
  • Delete the managed knowledge base and wait until it’s gone.
  • If you created the service role only for this evaluation, delete its inline policy, then the role.
  • With a customer managed key, check aws kms list-grants for grants Amazon Bedrock created, which can remain after the knowledge base is deleted.
  • Keep any S3 bucket that another knowledge base still reads.

Deletion protection on a managed data source limits how much a sync can delete, not whether you can delete the data source. Deleting the original knowledge base doesn’t delete its vector store, which continues to incur charges until you remove it. See Delete an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base.

Conclusion

With Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, your team no longer runs a vector store or manages the underlying retrieval infrastructure. With the migration guide in the amazon-bedrock skill, you ask your agent for a plan, review it, and approve only the resources you want built.

To get started, set up the Agent Toolkit for AWS and ask your agent for a read-only assessment of your knowledge base. After migration, explore agentic retrieval for multi-part questions. To learn more, see Build enterprise search for agents with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base on the AWS Machine Learning Blog.

About the authors

item.title: Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A…
item.description: Full title: Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS

Agents in multi-agent systems that span organizational boundaries often need to collaborate in a composable, interoperable way, with agents that other organizations build and run. They need a way to discover each other, communicate, and exchange tasks without exposing internals or requiring the same framework on both sides.

The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol addresses this constraint. Without A2A, building composable multi-agent systems across organizational boundaries requires custom integration code for each customer and framework. Independent software vendors (ISVs) can instead build composable, interoperable agents that work with the A2A-compatible frameworks their customers already use.

While we frame this post around the ISV use case, the pattern also applies to organizations that expose agents across boundaries, whether to partners, customers, or internal teams that use different frameworks. As your system grows, you add skills by registering Agent Cards with the orchestrator, without changing the agents already running.

In this post, we walk through a deployed reference architecture on AWS. A LangChain-based enterprise orchestrator communicates with a Strands Agents-based software as a service (SaaS) agent across organizational boundaries using A2A, with the enterprise and the SaaS provider in separate AWS accounts. Neither side depends on the other’s framework or SDK, and the two sides share no secrets. We cover the architecture and implementation patterns, then deploy the system from three Jupyter notebooks and run an end-to-end test.

The A2A protocol is now a Linux Foundation project, and AWS is among the organizations that support it. With A2A, agents can discover each other, negotiate tasks, and collaborate across organizational boundaries through a standardized protocol. The protocol uses existing authentication standards such as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) for cross-boundary security, and is designed to work across A2A-compatible frameworks.

In Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A, we introduced A2A concepts and demonstrated two Strands agents communicating using the protocol on AWS. That post established the foundation with Agent Card discovery, structured task execution, and the A2A server pattern. This post builds on that foundation with cross-framework interoperability, cross-organizational trust boundaries, and OAuth in both directions.

Solution overview

Three agents run in two AWS accounts, one for the enterprise and one for the SaaS provider. The A2A protocol connects them, with OAuth authentication in both directions. Each account has its own Amazon Cognito user pool, so each side authenticates with its own identity provider.

Figure 1: A2A agents across an enterprise account and a SaaS provider account

During onboarding, the enterprise and the SaaS provider exchange only public values, such as identity provider URLs, client IDs, scopes, and endpoint URLs. Each side then trusts tokens from the other side’s user pool, and no secrets are shared.

After onboarding, each request follows these steps:

  • The enterprise app gets an access token from the enterprise’s Amazon Cognito user pool.
  • The app sends a question over HTTPS to the user API in Amazon API Gateway, then polls for the answer.
  • Amazon API Gateway forwards the request privately, through a VPC link and an internal Network Load Balancer, to the Enterprise Orchestrator, a LangChain agent.
  • When its model decides that the question needs a compliance scan, the orchestrator gets its own token from the enterprise user pool, using a client secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager.
  • The orchestrator sends an A2A request to the compliance SaaS agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, using the skill it read from the agent’s Agent Card at startup.
  • The compliance agent checks the enterprise context agent’s Agent Card at the callback URL registered at onboarding, then gets a token from the SaaS provider’s own pool.
  • The compliance agent calls back to the enterprise context agent for account metadata, finishes its scan, and returns the answer to the orchestrator and then to the app.

On the enterprise side, two agents run on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate. The Enterprise Orchestrator is the entry point for users. LangChain provides the agent framework and tool-calling abstractions, and Amazon Bedrock provides the foundation models (FMs) that power each agent’s reasoning. The orchestrator uses LangChain and Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6). At startup, the orchestrator fetches the SaaS agent’s Agent Card from its well-known URL and creates a LangChain tool for each skill described on the card. The model then decides which tool to call based on the user’s question, so the orchestrator needs no hardcoded routing logic. It sends compliance scan requests over A2A with OAuth bearer tokens and summarizes the results for leadership. Users reach the orchestrator through an Amazon API Gateway HTTPS endpoint that accepts only tokens from the enterprise’s own pool.

The second enterprise agent provides internal context. The Enterprise Context Agent is built with LangChain and Amazon Bedrock (Amazon Nova Lite). It provides internal account metadata such as internal policy rules, data classification, business criticality, and escalation contacts (team on-call rotations). The deployed agent uses the official a2a-sdk (AgentCard, AgentExecutor, and spec-conformant JSON-RPC routes), pinned to a2a-sdk[http-server]==1.2.2. The SaaS agent reaches the context agent through an API Gateway partner API that accepts only the SaaS provider’s callback token.

Both enterprise agents run in private subnets of an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), with no public IP addresses.

On the SaaS provider side, the Compliance SaaS Agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in the SaaS provider’s own AWS account. Built with the Strands Agents SDK, it checks AWS accounts against the enterprise’s own internal policies, such as no public storage in production and encryption at rest for confidential data. In production, the scanning tools would connect to services such as AWS Config, AWS Security Hub, or Amazon GuardDuty. For this demo, the agent uses synthetic data that simulates compliance findings across multiple accounts.

Before it scans, the SaaS agent calls back to the Enterprise Context Agent for enterprise context, such as which accounts are production, which internal policies apply, and who to escalate to. This bidirectional pattern makes the agents true peers instead of a client and a server. The callback goes only to the address the customer registered at onboarding.

The key design decision is to use A2A for all cross-boundary communication. The enterprise has no access to the SaaS agent’s internal tools, system prompt, or model choice.
