Choose one clearly scoped business task and aim to establish an initial evaluation baseline within a week.

  • Days 1–2. Have the business owner and engineers agree on acceptance criteria, tiers, and thresholds. Prepare 20–30 golden examples covering common requests and important edge cases, with expected behavior approved by the business owner.
  • Days 3–5. Implement the evaluators described in section 5 and run the golden set repeatedly. Publish the baseline, including failures and the evidence needed to investigate them.
  • Week 2. Change one thing and re-evaluate under the same conditions. Record the release decision and its supporting evidence.

After reviewing the baseline, integrate evaluation into the release process and run it regularly to detect drift. Assign an owner to review production failures and feed confirmed cases back into the standard.

On AWS, use models available through Amazon Bedrock to build the agent. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, assesses agent behavior with built-in evaluators and supports custom evaluators for business-specific criteria. AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, provides execution visibility, complemented by Amazon CloudWatch for runtime monitoring and diagnostics. AgentCore runtime, Gateway, Identity, and Memory support execution, tool integration, identity management, and memory management.

About the authors

item.title: Build autonomous AI agents with Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Build autonomous AI agents with Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI

Java teams have established JVM tooling, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, and operational patterns, yet taking AI agents from prototype to production is hard: agent frameworks do not solve scalability, governance, security, and operational concerns by default. Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI close those gaps, so Java teams can build autonomous AI agents that plan, call tools and APIs, and maintain context across multi-turn conversations. Agentic AI is moving beyond prompt-response interactions toward autonomous systems that execute complex multi-step tasks.

Java remains one of the widely used programming languages in enterprise software. Teams have existing CI/CD pipelines, operational expertise, and established patterns built around the JVM. Spring AI brings AI capabilities to the JVM through familiar Spring patterns: auto-configuration, dependency injection, and composable advisors. Developers can build AI agents using the same idioms they use for REST APIs, security, and data access.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. With AgentCore, you can build, deploy, and operate AI agents at scale. It is framework-agnostic and model-agnostic: you bring your preferred agent framework and foundation model (FM). With AgentCore, you can access the production infrastructure you need: managed runtime, memory, browser automation, code execution, and identity management.

In this post, we show you how to build autonomous AI agents in Java using Spring AI and Amazon Bedrock with spring-ai-agentcore. We explore the key implementation patterns for two systems. The first is a single-agent travel assistant that demonstrates tool calling and memory. The second is a multi-agent intelligent document processing (IDP) system that shows how specialist agents, a rules engine, and alerting work together.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this walkthrough, you need the following:

  • Java – JDK 21 (required)
  • Spring Boot – 4.1 (with Spring AI 2.0 and spring-ai-agentcore 2.0)
  • Maven – 3.9+.
  • Node.js – 18+ (for the React frontend)
  • Terraform – 1.5+.
  • Docker – with Buildx for multi-architecture builds.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) – v2, configured with credentials.
  • An AWS account.

What makes a system an agent

A chat completion call can generate text, but it can’t decide what to do next, reach into external systems, or remember what happened yesterday. An agent can, because it unites three capabilities:

  • Planning – Given a goal, the model breaks it into steps, prioritizes them, and revises the plan as new information arrives.
  • Tool use – Beyond generating text, the model can select and invoke external functions such as APIs, databases, and code interpreters to act in the world.
  • Memory – Context carries across turns (short-term) and across sessions (long-term), so each decision builds on what came before.

A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application has limited tool use (retrieval) but no planning loop. An agent has all three, operating in a goal-directed loop until the task is complete or it determines it cannot proceed.

The following diagram shows these capabilities in an end-to-end agentic pipeline, from request to grounded answer.

Figure 1: Agentic reference architecture. A request flows through the runtime, guardrails, classification, a specialist agent, tools, the foundation model, memory, rules, and human review to a grounded answer, with resilience and observability as cross-cutting concerns

The pipeline has 11 stages. A client submits a document and question. The request passes through a runtime gateway for authentication and rate limiting, then input guardrails screen for harmful content. A router classifies the document and routes it to a specialist agent, which plans its workflow and calls tools, the Amazon Bedrock foundation model, memory, and a rules engine as needed. Low-confidence or flagged results go to a human review queue before the grounded answer returns to the client. Resilience, observability, logging, and least-privilege AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) apply across all stages.

Solution overview

The solution consists of two deployable systems that share common patterns:

  • Travel agent – A single autonomous agent with tool calling (weather lookups, itinerary search), streaming responses, conversation memory, and resilience patterns. This is the recommended starting point.
  • IDP multi-agent system – A multi-agent intelligent document processing platform with five specialist agents (Lawyer, Mortgage, Insurance, Tax, General), rules and workflow engine, alerting, and observability. This demonstrates production patterns at a scale.

Both systems share the following architecture:

  • Spring Boot application with Spring AI ChatClient, Spring AI agentcore and Amazon Bedrock Converse API.
  • AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, defines the contract (POST /invocations, GET /ping) for managed deployment.
  • Conversation memory through AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for both short-term and long-term context.
  • Tool calling with @Tool annotated methods.
  • Structured output mapped to Java records.
  • ARM64 container image optimized for AWS Graviton.
  • Modular Terraform for infrastructure provisioning.

The travel assistant is the recommended starting point. The following diagram illustrates how a Spring Boot agent interacts with AgentCore runtime, tools, memory, and models available on Amazon Bedrock.

Figure 2: Single-agent travel assistant. The Spring Boot application exposes both REST endpoints for the React UI and the AgentCore runtime contract, calling Amazon Bedrock through the Converse API while tool calling, streaming, and memory run inside one code base.

The travel assistant runs a single Spring Boot application with two entry points, the /invocations and /ping contract required by AgentCore runtime. Spring AI orchestrates calls to Amazon Bedrock through the Converse API and resolves tool invocations locally inside the same process. Server-Sent Events stream tokens to the client as they are generated. AgentCore memory supplies both short-term context within a session and long-term context across sessions, so the agent retains conversation history without external state management.

The following diagram shows the architecture for the IDP multi-agent system.

Figure 3: IDP multi-agent system architecture. Specialist agents process documents through a shared ChatClient pattern, with results flowing through a rules engine and alert service.

The IDP multi-agent system routes documents through five specialist agents (Lawyer, Mortgage, Insurance, Tax, and General), each built on a shared AbstractDocumentAgent template. A ClassifierAgent reads each document and forwards it to the appropriate specialist. The specialist extracts structured JSON with confidence scores using the multimodal Converse API of Amazon Bedrock. A rules engine evaluates Spring Expression Language (SpEL) expressions from application.yml against the extraction. ALERT or BLOCK severity rules dispatch through the AlertService. Low-confidence documents go to human review. Metrics, audit trail, resilience, and observability apply across all stages.

Agent collaboration patterns

When multiple agents work together, how they coordinate determines system behavior. This solution uses three patterns:

The following diagram compares the three coordination patterns used in this solution.

Figure 4: Agent collaboration patterns

Three patterns shown side by side. The router dispatches each request to one specialist by document type. The evaluator passes specialist findings through a rules engine that applies to severity levels and dispatches alerts or blocks for human review. The parallel fan-out sends one request to multiple specialists concurrently and aggregates results before the rules engine runs.

Router pattern: A lightweight orchestrator examines the incoming request and routes it to the appropriate specialist. In the IDP multi-agent system, the router inspects document type metadata and forwards it to the Lawyer, Mortgage, Insurance, Tax, or General agent. The router holds no domain logic. It is a dispatch layer only.

Parallel fan-out (optional extension): The base solution implements the router and evaluator patterns. The batch endpoint processes documents sequentially. When a document needs several perspectives at once, you can add a parallel fan-out as a drop-in extension. Dispatch to specialists concurrently and aggregate their results before the rules engine runs. Wall-clock time for the combined analysis is then bounded by the slowest single agent call rather than the sum of all calls.

Evaluator pattern: After specialists return their findings, a rules engine evaluates the combined output against configurable business rules. Rules that trigger ALERT or BLOCK severity dispatch through a pluggable AlertService for human review.

Walkthrough

The following sections walk you through the key implementation patterns, starting with the AgentCore runtime contract and progressing through tool calling, memory, resilience, and multi-agent orchestration.

Fulfilling the AgentCore runtime contract

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime manages agent lifecycle and scaling. For current rates, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing and Amazon Bedrock pricing. The runtime routes incoming requests to your agent and monitors its health. Your agent must expose two endpoints:

  • POST /invocations – Receives requests and returns responses as JSON or Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming.
  • GET /ping – Reports health status (Healthy or HealthyBusy). Long-running tasks must signal busy status, or the runtime might scale down the agent.

The following diagram shows how the Spring AI developer model maps onto AgentCore runtime, Memory, Browser, Code Interpreter, and Evaluations.

Figure 5: Spring AI AgentCore SDK on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Annotations, the ChatClient, tool callbacks, and advisors map through the spring-ai-agentcore SDK onto AgentCore runtime, AgentCore memory, AgentCore Browser, AgentCore Code Interpreter, and AgentCore Evaluations.

Two layers connected by the spring-ai-agentcore SDK. The application layer uses Spring AI components: @AgentCoreInvocation for endpoint wiring, ChatClient for model interaction, @Tool callbacks, and advisors for memory and guardrails. The infrastructure layer provides AgentCore runtime, AgentCore memory, AgentCore Browser, AgentCore Code Interpreter, and AgentCore Evaluations, all capabilities of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The SDK bridges both, so developers write standard Spring AI code while AgentCore handles production infrastructure.

With the Spring AI AgentCore SDK, a single annotation handles this contract automatically:

@Service
public class TravelAgent {
    private final ChatClient chatClient;

    public TravelAgent(ChatClient.Builder builder) {
        this.chatClient = builder.build();
    }

    @AgentCoreInvocation
    public Flux<String> chat(PromptRequest request) {
        return chatClient.prompt()
                .user(request.prompt())
                .stream()
                .content();
    }
}

The @AgentCoreInvocation annotation auto-configures the /invocations and /ping endpoints, handles JSON serialization, manages SSE framing for streaming responses, and reports health status. The same project also exposes REST endpoints for the React UI, so the agent serves both AgentCore runtime and a browser from one code base.

A note on streaming: the preceding minimal example returns the model stream directly, which is ideal for a chat UI. When an agent makes multi-argument tool calls, assemble the response with a blocking call() and then chunk the result for streaming, so the tool arguments bind reliably. The travel assistant serves both the AgentCore runtime and the React UI from one service method:

@RestController
public class AgentController {
    private final AgentService agentService;

    public AgentController(AgentService agentService) {
        this.agentService = agentService;
    }

    // One annotation wires up POST /invocations + GET /ping, JSON/SSE framing, and health.
    @AgentCoreInvocation
    public Flux<String> invoke(PromptRequest request, AgentCoreContext context) {
        String sessionId = context.getHeader(AgentCoreHeaders.SESSION_ID);
        return agentService.streamChat(request.prompt(), sessionId,
                request.guardrailsEnabled(), request.memoryEnabled());
    }

    // The same app also serves the React UI from the same code base.
    @PostMapping(value = "/api/chat", produces = MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN_VALUE + ";charset=UTF-8")
    public Flux<String> chatStream(@Valid @RequestBody PromptRequest request) {
        return agentService.streamChat(request.prompt(), request.sessionId(),
                request.guardrailsEnabled(), request.memoryEnabled());
    }
}

Implementing tool calling

With tool calling, the model can invoke external functions during reasoning. In Spring AI, you annotate a method with @Tool and the model decides when to call it and with what arguments:

@Tool(description = "Get a short weather forecast for a city")
public String getWeather(
        @ToolParam(description = "City name") String city) {
    return forecastService.lookup(city);
}

You register tools on the ChatClient, and the model decides when to call them:

ChatClient chatClient = chatClientBuilder
        .defaultSystem(properties.getSystemPrompt())
        .defaultTools(new DateTimeTools(), new TravelTools())
        .build();

For structured output, request a Java record type. For multimodal input, attach media to the user message:

ProcessedDocument review = chatClient.prompt()
        .system(personaSystemPrompt)
        .user(u -> u.text(question).media(mimeType, fileResource))
        .call()
        .entity(ProcessedDocument.class);

Note: We verified this example with Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Amazon Bedrock. Spring AI adds the record’s schema to the prompt and parses the reply back into the Java type. Behavior can differ for other model families, so refer to the Spring AI structured output documentation and the Amazon Bedrock documentation for current support. It is best-effort, meaning that models can occasionally return output that does not match the schema. For stricter results, use a provider with native schema enforcement or Spring AI validation and retry.

The model receives the tool definitions as part of its context, reasons about when a tool call would help satisfy the user request, and returns a structured tool call response. Spring AI intercepts this, invokes the annotated method, and feeds the result back to the model for further reasoning.

Adding conversation memory

Real-world agents must remember what users said earlier in a conversation (working memory) and what they have learned over time (persistent memory). The Spring AI AgentCore SDK integrates with AgentCore memory through the advisor pattern: interceptors that enrich prompts with context before they reach the model.

chatClient.prompt()
        .advisors(agentCoreMemory.advisors)
        .advisors(a -> a.param(
                ChatMemory.CONVERSATION_ID, "user:" + sessionId))
        .user(prompt)
        .stream()
        .content();

The session ID becomes a conversation ID in actor:session form, so each user’s history stays isolated. For user-facing deployments, derive the actor from a verified OAuth 2.0 (JWT) identity rather than a client-supplied value, so users cannot access one another’s history.

In addition, AgentCore memory offers long-term memory support, employing the following strategies to identify and capture key insights from conversations:

  • Semantic – Factual information about users (for example, “User works in finance”)
  • User preference – Explicit settings and choices (for example, “Metric units preferred”)
  • Summary – Condensed conversation history for continuity across sessions.
  • Episodic – Past interactions and lessons learned.

Long-term memory extraction is asynchronous and optional. You choose which strategies to enable when you create the memory, and AgentCore extracts and consolidates records in the background after each conversation, so it never blocks the agent’s response. Choose strategies by workload: use user preference for the travel assistant so it remembers units and seating choices. Use summary when sessions span many turns. Use episodic when the agent should reuse lessons from past tasks. And use semantic to retain durable facts about the user.

Configuring the rules engine

Reading a document is only half the job. Acting on what it finds is the other half. The IDP multi-agent system includes a rules engine so operators can add business checks without touching code. This is an in-process rules evaluator that applies SpEL conditions to extraction results, not a workflow orchestration service such as AWS Step Functions. Rules live in application.yml and each condition is a SpEL expression evaluated against the extraction:

idp:
  review:
    enabled: ${REVIEW_ENABLED:true}
    confidence-threshold: ${REVIEW_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD:0.7}
    rules:
      - id: legal-unsigned
        agentType: LAWYER
        condition: "field('signaturePresent') == 'false' || missing('signaturePresent')"
        severity: ALERT
        message: "Document appears unsigned; get all parties to sign before relying on it."
      - id: mortgage-high-dti
        agentType: MORTGAGE
        condition: "field('dtiRatio') != '' && T(java.lang.Double).parseDouble(field('dtiRatio')) > 0.43"
        severity: WARN
        message: "Debt-to-income ratio exceeds 0.43; likely needs manual underwriting."
      - id: low-confidence
        agentType: ALL
        condition: "confidence < 0.6"
        severity: WARN
        message: "Low extraction confidence; consider human verification."

Severity levels control the engine’s behavior. INFO and WARN are logged, while ALERT dispatches through a pluggable AlertService. The default logs and emits a metric, but you can substitute Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), Slack, or email by providing your own bean. BLOCK holds the document for manual review. Because rules are operator configuration rather than end user input, they provide a safe and auditable extension point. Adding new workflows is a configuration change, not a deployment.

The evaluator pattern is implemented by the rules engine and a pluggable AlertService. The default implementation logs the alert and emits a metric. You provide your own bean to route to Amazon SNS, Slack, or email:

public class LoggingAlertService implements AlertService {
    @Override
    public void send(RuleResult result, AgentType agentType, ProcessedDocument document) {
        registry.counter("idp.alerts.sent",
                "severity", result.severity().name(), "type", agentType.name()).increment();
        logger.warn("ALERT [{}] rule={} type={} message=\"{}\"",
                result.severity(), result.ruleId(), agentType, result.message());
    }
}

Production readiness patterns

The following patterns address common production requirements that prototypes typically skip.

Resilience

Every model call uses a Resilience4j retry with exponential backoff, a circuit breaker that fails fast when model calls repeatedly fail or time out, and a timeout. Streaming paths emit a fallback message instead of a raw error. When traffic exceeds your account and Region service quotas, AgentCore runtime returns HTTP 429 and the retry handles it. For current limits, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore quotas documentation.

Twelve-factor configurations

Every configurable value (Region, model ID, memory ID, timeouts, rate limits, system prompt) is an environment variable bound to a typed @ConfigurationProperties class. The application is stateless, starts fast, drains in-flight turns on scale-down, and ships as one immutable ARM64 image promoted unchanged from development to production.

Security and identity

The Agentcore runtime uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) authentication by default. For user-facing agents, add an OAuth 2.0 (JWT) authorizer (such as Amazon Cognito) and derive the memory actor ID (actorId) from the verified identity. The IAM execution role follows least privilege:

  • Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) pull.
  • Scoped Amazon CloudWatch Logs and AWS X-Ray.
  • Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel actions.
  • Scoped workload access tokens (GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT) for the agent’s workload identity.
  • AgentCore memory actions limited to the specific Memory resource ARN.

AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, enforces inbound authentication (acting as an OAuth 2.0 resource server that validates JWT bearer tokens through Cognito, Okta, Auth0, or your own OIDC provider) and supports configurable rate limiting at the gateway layer. Rate limits are fail-open by default, so they should complement your core security controls rather than replace them.

Responsible AI controls

Autonomous agents that take real-world actions need safety controls as a first-class concern. The sample ships with a stand-in demonstration of a lightweight in-process pre-check called GuardrailService. This service screens prompts for disallowed intent and prompt injection, toggled per request with the guardrailsEnabled flag. Production deployments use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails as a standard control applied to every request, not a per-request toggle.

To upgrade the demo service for production, front the agent with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Guardrails apply configurable policies outside the model call, covering both input and output:

  • Content filtering. Blocks harmful or off-topic content based on configurable thresholds for both prompts and responses.
  • Denied topics. Prevents the agent from engaging with topics you define as out-of-scope.
  • Sensitive information filters. Detects and redacts PII in both prompts and responses, supporting requirements such as GDPR and HIPAA.

For agents that retrieve external knowledge, enable grounding checks to reduce hallucination risk before the agent acts on tool calls with real-world side effects.

To wire Bedrock Guardrails into Spring AI, implement CallAdvisor and StreamAdvisor functions that call the ApplyGuardrail API and register it with defaultAdvisors on the ChatClient. Because policies live in the guardrail, security teams can update filters independently of the application release cycle.

Observability

The example instruments with the Micrometer Observation API (@Observed), producing timers that become distributed trace spans when you add a tracing bridge (OTLP to AWS X-Ray). The system emits domain metrics:

idp.documents.processed{type,status}
idp.extraction.confidence{type}
idp.alerts.sent{severity,type}
idp.processing.duration{type}

These metrics are exposed through /actuator/prometheus. The application also emits structured JSON logs to standard output, which Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime captures in Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

Optional extension that’s not implemented in this post: The sample includes the Micrometer OpenTelemetry bridge and OTLP exporter dependencies, but this post’s deployment does not provision an OpenTelemetry collector or enable trace sampling. You can add distributed tracing by setting a nonzero TRACING_SAMPLING value, pointing OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT to an OpenTelemetry or AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry collector, and configuring the collector to forward traces to AWS X-Ray.

Optional extension that’s not implemented in this post: The sample doesn’t implement an automated evaluation or optimization feedback loop. You can add one by persisting application metrics, traces, audit events, and human-review outcomes as an evaluation dataset. AgentCore evaluations or a separate evaluation pipeline can then compare versioned prompts, models, tools, and routing rules against quality, safety, latency, and cost thresholds. Promote changes only after evaluation and human approval.

Deploying the solution

This GitHub repository contains two AI agent applications demonstrating different use cases for autonomous AI. This guide shows you how to deploy them to AWS using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime.

The following diagram shows the deployment architecture: a single Arm64 image promoted through modular Terraform to the AgentCore runtime, with an optional Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) path.

Optional: running on Amazon EKS. Teams already standardized on Kubernetes can run the same Arm64 image on Amazon EKS, using their existing cluster for scaling and health checks against the /ping endpoint, with IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) for scoped, least-privilege pod-level access to Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore memory. The container is identical, so nothing in the application changes.

Figure 6: Deployment architecture. Modular Terraform provisions Amazon ECR, a least-privilege IAM execution role, and the Bedrock AgentCore runtime, with an optional Amazon EKS and IRSA path that reuses the same Arm64 image.

Three stages: build and publish, Terraform, and runs on AWS. The CI pipeline packages the application into a linux/arm64 image and pushes it to Amazon ECR with immutable tags. Three Terraform modules provision the ECR repository, a least-privilege IAM execution role, and the AgentCore runtime. The agent runs serverlessly on AgentCore runtime, calling Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore memory. An optional Amazon EKS path reuses the same image with IRSA for scoped pod-level credentials.

Follow these steps to deploy either application.

Step 1: Clone the repository

Open your terminal and run:

git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-build-autonomous-ai-agents-with-amazon-bedrock-and-spring-ai.git

Step 2: Navigate to the directory for the agent you want to deploy

  • Deploy autonomous agent: cd build-autonomous-ai-agents-with-amazon-bedrock-and-spring-ai/code/autonomous-agent
  • Deploy IDP multi-agent system: cd build-autonomous-ai-agents-with-amazon-bedrock-and-spring-ai/code/idp-agent

Step 3: Configure Terraform variables

Before deploying the infrastructure, configure your Terraform variables in the terraform.tfvars file located in the terraform directory.

Basic configuration

The solution uses default values for most settings, but you can customize the following in your terraform.tfvars file:

  • AWS Region: The AWS Region where resources are deployed.
  • Environment: Environment ID (such as dev or prod) used in resource naming.
  • bedrock_model: Amazon Bedrock foundation model (for example: global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0). For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

Step 4: Run the deployment script

For Linux/macOS:

./scripts/deploy.sh dev

For Windows PowerShell:

.\scripts\deploy.ps1 dev

The deployment script does the following:

  • Create an Amazon ECR repository.
  • Build the Java application.
  • Create and push a Docker container image.
  • Create an IAM execution role.
  • Deploy the AgentCore runtime.

Step 5: Run the application

Once the deployment is complete, you can run the application using the following commands.

For Linux/macOS:

./scripts/run.sh dev

For Windows PowerShell:

.\scripts\run.ps1 dev

Cleaning up

AgentCore runtime scales to zero and bills per invocation, so an idle agent costs almost nothing. Your main variable cost is Amazon Bedrock token usage, plus a small amount for Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon ECR storage. For current rates, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing and Amazon Bedrock pricing. To avoid incurring future charges, tear down the infrastructure when you are finished:

For Linux/macOS:

./scripts/cleanup.sh dev

For Windows PowerShell:

.\scripts\cleanup.ps1 dev

Delete any AgentCore memory resources and Amazon ECR images you no longer need using the AWS CLI.

Conclusion

In this post, you learned how to build autonomous AI agents in Java using Spring AI and Amazon Bedrock. We covered the three capabilities that turn a model into an agent: planning, tool use, and memory. We also showed how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore services carry an agent to production. The Spring AI AgentCore SDK maps these capabilities onto idiomatic Spring through annotations and a familiar ChatClient. Finally, we outlined architecture patterns for multi-agent collaboration. These include the router pattern, the evaluator pattern implemented by the rules engine, and parallel fan-out as an optional extension.

The key takeaway for Java teams: you do not need to leave your environment to build production-quality agents. The patterns you already trust (dependency injection, configuration properties, advisors, Actuator, Micrometer) carry directly into the agentic world. AgentCore supplies the runtime, memory, identity, and governance that production demands.

As next steps, consider the following:

  • Connect enterprise systems through AgentCore Gateway and the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
  • Add Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed RAG capability, and web search so the agent reasons over your data.
  • Implement Amazon Cognito JWT authentication with per-user memory isolation.
  • Customize Amazon Bedrock Guardrails policies: add domain-specific denied topics, tighten content-filtering thresholds, and enable grounding checks tuned to your knowledge sources.
  • Use AgentCore Evaluations to score production traces and promote prompt or model changes after review.

Each is an incremental addition to the foundation you have built here, not a rewrite.

About the authors

item.title: OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock

Developers increasingly use Codex with Amazon Bedrock to explore unfamiliar code, make changes, and handle repetitive engineering work. For platform teams, the challenge is to make those tools available without creating a second model-access, identity, and operations stack.

Codex can use Amazon Bedrock for inference with supported OpenAI models. In this post, we show how to fit that path into the AWS identity, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Regional, and observability practices your organization already uses. Codex still runs on the developer workstation. The main design choice is how its model requests reach Amazon Bedrock and where your organization applies policy and operational controls.

We begin with a small, least-privilege pilot and work through the checks that matter before access expands. The examples use GPT-5.6 Sol. Before starting the pilot, review Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock to confirm that Sol, Terra, or Luna is available in the AWS Region and inference path you plan to use.

Recommended default: Start with Native AWS Access for a small, least-privilege pilot. Choose AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, when you want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Choose an LLM Gateway when a platform team wants to enforce controls in the request path. A custom integration is the advanced version of the LLM Gateway pattern, not a quick start.

The examples come from the open source Guidance for Codex on AWS repository. It includes quick starts for Native AWS Access, AgentCore Gateway, LiteLLM on ECS, Portkey, the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT), and the Amazon CloudWatch setup used later in the post. Choose the quick start that matches your architecture, use it for the pilot, and adapt it to your environment.

Choose your rollout path

Authentication is only one part of an enterprise rollout. Decide who can use the service and which models and Regions are approved. Also define where configuration lives, what telemetry to collect, how usage is allocated, and which skills or Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are allowed. The following table maps those needs to an access path and an owning team.

Choose the access path that provides the controls you need now. The most straightforward path that meets the requirement usually has the lowest operational overhead.

Decision rules

  • Native AWS Access is the usual starting point when AWS identity and IAM controls are enough for the pilot.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Within the platform, AgentCore Gateway fits teams that want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for routing, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, or related controls.
  • A large language model (LLM) Gateway fits organizations that already operate a gateway or want to enforce controls in the request path. Building a custom gateway is the advanced version of this option.

The following diagram compares where identity, routing, policy, telemetry, and operational ownership sit across the three rollout paths.

Figure 1: Codex runs on the developer workstation in each scenario. Native AWS Access uses AWS IAM Identity Center, a configured AgentCore Gateway can apply managed routing and Guardrails, and a configured LLM Gateway can apply request-path controls

Native AWS Access

If Native AWS Access fits the pilot, the repository’s Native AWS Access quick start provides the complete procedure and supporting files. The following abbreviated walkthrough focuses on the sequence and the checks that matter most.

Use your workforce identity provider for sign-in

Employees continue to sign in through the identity provider they already use. In this example, Okta handles authentication through Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) and provisions users and groups into IAM Identity Center through System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM). IAM Identity Center then issues the temporary AWS credentials used by Codex. The identity provider is not configured in Codex.

Prerequisites

  • Add each pilot user to a dedicated group in the workforce identity system and provision that group to IAM Identity Center. Keep the assignment limited to the pilot.
  • Choose an Amazon Bedrock Region and an OpenAI model available to the pilot identity, plus an inference profile if the selected API requires one. Check Sol, Terra, and Luna separately for the chosen account, Region, and inference path.
  • Grant only the Amazon Bedrock model inference permissions used by Codex, any direct validation commands, and the selected observability destination.
  • Prepare a non-production repository and name a rollback owner.

Configure

The pilot has three checks. First, sign in using the IAM Identity Center profile configured for the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and call Amazon Bedrock Runtime directly. Next, point Codex to the approved model. Finally, run a safe Codex task. The direct call isolates AWS access problems. The final step confirms the Codex configuration.

Step 1: Sign in and validate Amazon Bedrock Runtime access.

aws sso login --profile codex-bedrock
export AWS_PROFILE=codex-bedrock
aws bedrock-runtime converse
--model-id us.openai.gpt-5.6-sol
--messages '[{"role":"user","content":[{"text":"Reply with OK"}]}]'
--region us-east-2

This command creates a short-lived AWS session and checks whether the profile can invoke the chosen model in the chosen Region. If it fails, resolve the profile, Region, model or inference-profile access, or IAM permissions before configuring Codex.

Step 2: Configure the Codex provider.

# ~/.codex/config.toml (or managed user configuration)
model_provider = "amazon-bedrock"
model = "openai.gpt-5.6-sol"

[model_providers.amazon-bedrock.aws]
profile = "codex-bedrock"
region = "us-east-2"

The model value is the Codex model ID. The profile selects the AWS IAM Identity Center session, and region tells Codex which AWS Region to use. Keep these settings in user-level or managed configuration so a repository cannot change the provider.

Verify the pilot and confirm rollback

Before adding users, make sure the pilot reaches the approved model, produces the expected records, and can be disabled cleanly.

  • Identity: aws sts get-caller-identity returns the expected IAM Identity Center assumed-role session.
  • Model access: The pilot profile invokes the approved model through the API and Region selected for the test.
  • Codex access: The user completes a safe, read-only task in a non-production repository, and the expected request-path evidence is available.
  • Evidence and rollback: The identity, invocation, audit, and optional telemetry records are present. Remove the configuration or IAM Identity Center assignment, handle any active session according to your procedure or wait for it to expire, and verify that a new invocation is denied.

Watch the Native AWS Access walkthrough

The walkthrough shows the complete pilot sequence: workforce sign-in, direct Amazon Bedrock Runtime validation, Codex provider configuration, and a safe test task.

Figure 2: Native AWS Access walkthrough covering workforce sign-in, Amazon Bedrock Runtime validation, Codex provider configuration, and a safe pilot task

Use the video to verify the order of the checks and the evidence to collect before adding more pilot users.

Run a two-user identity-isolation check

Two users are required to test identity isolation. A single user shows that sign-in works. A second user tests whether attribution remains distinct. Have two pilot users sign in separately and run the same harmless task. Their assumed-role sessions and audit records, and telemetry records if configured, should remain distinct.

The following diagram shows how separate pilot identities should produce separate AWS sessions, request evidence, and optional telemetry while using the same approved Codex and Amazon Bedrock path.

Figure 3: Use trusted identity enrollment for attribution. A local collector can add approved identity context only when it is deployed and configured as part of a managed enrollment process

Gateway paths for request-path controls

AgentCore Gateway is an option when you want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for centralized routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. If your organization already runs an LLM Gateway or wants to enforce controls in the request path, use that gateway instead. Validate the selected gateway before exposing it to pilot users.

LLM Gateway: Validate before a pilot

  • Check that the gateway accepts the Codex request format.
  • Use the sign-in or token flow defined by the gateway team.
  • Before inviting pilot users, test model routing, monitoring, failure handling, and rollback.

Custom enterprise integration

A custom enterprise integration is the most involved form of the LLM Gateway pattern. Consider it only when Native AWS Access, AgentCore Gateway, and an existing gateway cannot meet a specific requirement. The result is another service to design, secure, test, support, and operate, so platform engineering and security need to own it from the start.

Observe, govern, and allocate cost

Codex OpenTelemetry, Amazon Bedrock service records, AWS identity records, and billing data answer different questions. Codex OpenTelemetry describes client activity. Amazon Bedrock service metrics and model invocation logs show service-side activity when enabled. AWS identity records and the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) provide identity and billed-usage evidence. Correlate them for the path you deploy, and do not present token volume as a cost report.

Define what code, prompts, files, and tool output Codex might send through the selected model path. Exclude secrets and restricted data unless the organization has approved that data flow. Require developers to review and test generated changes before merge. Telemetry does not establish correctness or safety.

OpenTelemetry metrics from Codex

For observability, this post uses the ADOT collector configuration and CloudWatch dashboard from the repository’s monitoring and operations guidance. Deploy that configuration to each managed pilot device, then run a safe Codex task.

The repository provides the configuration files. Follow its deployment instructions to install the approved ADOT collector and configure its AWS authentication.

# ~/.codex/config.toml or managed user configuration
[otel]
environment = "pilot"
log_user_prompt = false
metrics_exporter = { "otlp-http" = { endpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:4318/v1/metrics", protocol = "binary" } }

Validate the repository path: run a safe Codex task and confirm that the expected operational metrics appear on the managed CloudWatch dashboard.

Telemetry planeExamplesAttribution boundary
Codex OpenTelemetry metricsToken usage, turns, API requests, request duration, tool calls, session source.Per-user and team dashboard grouping only after the local collector adds validated identity attributes.
Amazon Bedrock service metricsInvocations, latency, input tokens, output tokens, client errors, server errors.Use the documented namespace, metric names, and dimensions for the selected Runtime, Mantle, or AgentCore path.
AWS identity evidence, model invocation logs, and CURAssumed-role single sign-on (SSO) principal plus billed Bedrock line items.For Native IAM Identity Center access, CUR 2.0 with caller-identity allocation can expose the SSO principal. Gateway paths require gateway telemetry and spend records for end-user allocation.

Amazon CloudWatch dashboard and evidence

The Amazon CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights managed dashboard in the Guidance for Codex on AWS repository shows Codex operational metrics collected through ADOT. Use it to understand client activity, and use AWS identity, audit, and billing records separately when you need attribution or cost evidence.

QuestionDecisionEvidence to keep
Who invoked the model?Use the AWS identity/audit source for the path you selected.Pilot identity record and request correlation, where available.
What did it cost?Use billing data for actual charge and label any inferred allocation clearly.CUR source, allocation method, and known uncertainty.
Can we stop unsafe or expensive behavior?Use alarms for detection. Use IAM and managed client controls for their respective access and action boundaries. Use gateway policy when request-path enforcement, such as hard budgets or rate limits, is required.Control test results and rollback procedure.

Watch the Codex OTel and CloudWatch walkthrough

The walkthrough shows how to query Codex OpenTelemetry metrics and confirm that the expected token and request data appears in Amazon CloudWatch.

Figure 4: Codex OpenTelemetry metrics shown in an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard

The example validates the aliased metric result in Amazon CloudWatch Query Studio and shows how the dashboard represents Codex client activity.

Standardize team behavior

After the infrastructure path is working, turn to the developer experience. Repository guidance, managed plugins, hooks, and approved MCP servers can make the rollout consistent without asking each team to assemble its own setup.

Plugins

Organization-owned plugins are a practical way to distribute shared skills, hooks, and approved MCP integrations. Give each plugin an owner and version, review changes before release, and publish it only through approved sources. Test updates with a pilot group and keep a documented removal path.

A plugin might include an MCP server configuration, but that does not make every bundled tool approved. Allow only the servers and tools the organization has reviewed, with user confirmation where it is needed.

Hooks

Hooks can be declared in hooks.json or directly in configuration. Keep the documented event casing, and deploy organization-owned policy commands through approved endpoint tooling.

[[hooks.PreToolUse]]
matcher = "^Bash$"

[[hooks.PreToolUse.hooks]]
type = "command"
command = "/usr/local/bin/company-pre-tool-policy"
timeout = 30

Use PreToolUse, PostToolUse, or SessionStart where they solve a specific need. Before wider deployment, test allow, deny, timeout, and disconnected-endpoint behavior.

MCP

An MCP server connects Codex to another system, so each server creates a separate trust boundary. Limit access to the users and tools that need it, manage credentials through an approved OAuth or secrets process, and require confirmation for tools that change external systems. Keep MCP credentials out of the model-provider configuration.

Roll out in phases

The following diagram defines the scope and evidence required to advance from preparation through pilot, expansion, and organization-wide standardization.

Figure 5: Start with a controlled pilot, expand after validating the access path and operational evidence, and standardize the rollout after the operating model is proven

Administrator launch checklist

  • Record the selected path, owning team, Region, and model in the change record.
  • Limit the pilot identity to the required permissions, and document how issued credentials or tokens are handled.
  • Run a non-production test that covers sign-in, model availability, and one safe Codex task.
  • Check telemetry and audit output from the deployed version rather than assuming the example applies unchanged.
  • Separate billed amounts from estimates in cost reporting.
  • Exercise recovery: remove the configuration or assignment, handle any active session through the approved procedure or wait for it to expire, and verify that a new invocation is denied.

Clean up

When the pilot ends or access must be disabled, remove the rollout resources that are no longer required.

Remove the Codex model-provider and telemetry configuration from managed devices. Remove the IAM Identity Center pilot assignment or gateway access, revoke pilot tokens and secrets, and handle active sessions according to the approved procedure. Uninstall or disable the ADOT collector, and delete the pilot CloudWatch dashboard and alarms if they are not shared with another workload. Verify cleanup by confirming that a new model invocation is denied and that retired telemetry resources receive no new data.

Configuration boundaries

Keep model-provider, credential, and organization telemetry settings in user-level or managed configuration. Project-local .codex/config.toml is repository-scoped configuration: Review it as code, but do not treat it as an enterprise enforcement boundary. AGENTS.md is useful for durable repository guidance, such as test commands and coding conventions, but it is not an enforcement boundary either.

Setting typeRecommended locationReason
Model provider, credentials, RegionUser-level or managed configurationThese are endpoint and enterprise choices, not repository defaults.
OpenTelemetry exporterUser-level or managed configurationTelemetry destination and data handling are organization controls.
Repository instructionsAGENTS.mdCarries durable guidance but is not an enforcement boundary.
Permission requirementsOrganization-managed requirements.tomlConstrains supported security-sensitive client choices.

Conclusions and next steps

Codex can use Amazon Bedrock for inference with supported OpenAI models. Start with the least-complex access path that meets the requirement, prove the identity and model path with a small pilot, and add gateway or client controls only when they solve a specific need.

AgentCore Gateway provides an AWS managed gateway option for routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Choose an LLM Gateway when a platform team wants to enforce controls in the request path. Build a custom integration only when the available paths cannot meet a documented requirement.

Expand in stages and use evidence from each stage to decide what comes next. The Guidance for Codex on AWS repository contains the maintained configurations and validation procedures used in this post.

About the authors

item.title: Semantic diffing of formal policies with anti-unification
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Semantic diffing of formal policies with anti-unification

When reviewing code, you start with a diff. You wouldn’t compare two 3,000-line files by eye and hope to spot every change. Formal policies can be even harder to compare because a textual diff often highlights syntactic changes that don’t affect meaning. Reorder two conjuncts, swap the arguments of an equality, or use an equivalent predicate, and much of the file might appear changed. A real change in behavior, such as an Or where the requirement says and, can get lost in that noise.

A semantic diff shows what two policies have in common and where they disagree. The open source engine used in this post computes this diff using anti-unification, which finds a most specific common pattern for two expressions. Plotkin’s 1970 paper gives the classical formulation. The engine works over an e-graph, which keeps track of expressions known to be equal. We supply the algebraic laws and domain rules that justify those equalities, such as equating an external destination with one that isn’t internal. The result shows the shared parts once and keeps both versions of each differing part for review. If no differences remain, the policies are equivalent under those laws and rules. When the rules or the search are incomplete, a remaining difference might reflect an equivalence the engine has not found.

One use case is autoformalization. Autoformalization translates natural language into a formal language. Suppose you want to turn requirements into SMT-LIB, the standard input language for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers such as Z3 and cvc5, or into Cedar or Dogwood to control authorization in your software system. A large language model (LLM) generates the formal artifact from the prose. The model writes the artifact. It plays no part in computing the diff. Run the model twice, and it might produce two different formalizations, with no ground truth to identify the correct one. A semantic diff shows where they agree and where they differ. Generate more candidates by varying the model, prompt, or sampling temperature. Comparing them shows which parts stay the same and which vary. Review the varying parts first.

Requirements can also become OpenShell sandbox policies or Common Expression Language (CEL) expressions. OpenShell uses YAML to describe an agent’s filesystem and network access. CEL is embedded in applications to evaluate expressions, including policy conditions. These languages and formats differ in what they express, but translations into any of them can disagree about a condition, a scope, or an event. The following table gives illustrative disagreements:

Language or formatPolicy focusExample disagreement
CedarWho can perform an action on a resource, under which conditions.One translation requires ownership and approval. Another accepts either.
DogwoodAuthorization involving the current request and recent event history.One translation checks a successful prior response. Another checks a request event.
OpenShell policiesAn agent’s filesystem and network access, including rules for particular binaries.One translation permits repository-scoped GET. Another permits organization-scoped POST.
CELConditions evaluated over inputs supplied by a host application.One translation requires production for both allowed ports. Another requires it for only one.

In each worked example, we compare translations of the same requirement within one policy context. We encode the relevant syntax as terms and declare the equalities used in the comparison. The engine reads these encodings. It doesn’t import native policies from the four formats.

The idea is a formal-methods analogue of semantic entropy, described by Farquhar et al. in Nature (2024). That approach samples several natural-language answers, clusters those that entail one another, and reports a single number. For formal outputs, anti-unification preserves more information. It identifies the shared structure and each divergence instead of returning only a score.

Counterexamples help explain the consequences of a disagreement. An SMT solver can find a concrete assignment that satisfies one formula and violates the other. A reviewer can then trace that assignment through the formulas to understand the conflicting decisions. The anti-unifier gives a different view: it organizes the shared structure and the fragments that differ, without issuing an SMT query. A solver or policy validator can help resolve those fragments. We assume you can read S-expression syntax, as in SMT-LIB, and know what an authorization policy is. E-graphs and anti-unification are explained as they come up.

When several translations agree on part of a requirement, the diff shows that part once. Where they disagree, it keeps the alternatives visible for review.

How semantic diffing represents disagreement

Say a policy-generation pipeline hands you two candidate rules for this requirement: sensitive data sent to an external destination must be encrypted.

Rule ARule B
sensitive(data) ∧ external(dst) → encrypted¬internal(dst) ∧ sensitive(data) → audited

Whether these are the same rule isn’t obvious. The conditions are reordered, external is expressed indirectly as not internal, and the conclusions do not match. The engine computes a most specific anti-unifier for these terms. In its input language, the two rules are S-expressions.

The complete program first declares the vocabulary:

(sort Formula)
(sort Data)
(sort Dest)
(function Lit (bool) Formula)
(function And (Formula) Formula :assoc-comm-idem :identity (Lit true))
(function Implies (Formula Formula) Formula)
(function Not (Formula) Formula)

It then adds one function line for each predicate (sensitive, external, internal) and constant (data, dst, encrypted, audited). Here, And is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent, as the next section explains:

(let ruleA (Implies (And (sensitive (data)) (external (dst)))
                    (encrypted)))
(let ruleB (Implies (And (Not (internal (dst))) (sensitive (data)))
                    (audited)))

(antiunify ruleA ruleB :algorithm exact)

The engine answers with a single term:

(anti-unify :size 11 :cr 0.5000 :completion exact
  (Implies
    (And (sensitive data) (Variants (external dst) (Not (internal dst))))
    (Variants encrypted audited)))

The reordering doesn’t appear in the result because And is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent. Two Variants nodes remain, each marking a place where the inputs disagree, and only one of them is a difference in meaning. The difference between (external dst) and (Not (internal dst)) is a difference in vocabulary. Both express the same domain fact. The engine can’t infer that from syntax alone. State the domain fact as a rewrite, run it to saturation (until no rule adds a new equality), and diff again:

(rewrite (external d) (Not (internal d)))
(run 2)
(antiunify ruleA ruleB :algorithm exact)

After saturation, the engine answers:

(anti-unify :size 8 :cr 0.1429 :completion exact
  (Implies (And (sensitive data) (external dst)) (Variants encrypted audited)))

One Variants node remains: Rule B audits where the requirement demands encryption. A textbook presentation would put a fresh variable at that spot. The engine instead writes (Variants encrypted audited): a node that holds both readings. Select the first child of every Variants node and you reconstruct rule A, up to the declared algebra and rewrites. Select the second child and you get rule B. The anti-unifier is a lossless merge of both terms: Shared structure appears once, and every genuine disagreement is a localized, reviewable node.

Three fields describe the result: :size, :cr, and :completion. The :size field counts the concrete nodes (a Variants marker itself isn’t counted, but both of its children are, so structure can’t hide inside one).

The :cr field reports the compression ratio (s - a) / b, where s is the result size and a and b are the smaller and larger input sizes. For each input, we use its smallest known equivalent form in the current e-graph. A score of 0 means full agreement under the declared equalities.

After the preceding rewrite, both inputs have seven nodes and the result has eight, giving (8 - 7) / 7, or approximately 0.1429. Keeping both complete policies in a single Variants node would use fourteen nodes, giving (14 - 7) / 7 = 1. This is the reference value for no sharing.

A score of 1 is a reference value, not an upper bound. The search might use larger equivalent forms than the smallest known inputs. A result larger than their combined sizes therefore scores above 1. For example, if both smallest input forms have ten nodes and a result has twenty-three, the ratio is (23 - 10) / 10 = 1.3.

The :completion field reports exact when the search space was exhausted and budget when the default anytime search (a Monte Carlo search, described in the implementation section) reached its playout limit before exhausting the search space.

A low :cr means the inputs share more structure under the declared equalities. It doesn’t establish correctness: two candidates can share the same mistake. An entropy score summarizes variation in one number. The full semantic diff also identifies where the candidates disagree and retains both alternatives in Variants nodes.

A semantic diff ignores only the differences covered by the declared equalities. A plain syntactic anti-unifier would also have reported the reordering in this example. The next three sections show how to declare the algebra and add domain identities.

The anti-unifier stores shared structure once and marks each disagreement with a Variants node. Selecting one side of every node reconstructs the corresponding input, modulo the declared equalities.

Run a semantic diff in 5 minutes

The engine requires only a pinned Rust toolchain to build from source. Its formal-verification annotations, covered in the implementation section, compile away under plain rustc. These commands pin the revision used for the worked examples:

git clone https://github.com/yaspar-org/semi-persistent.git
cd semi-persistent
git fetch origin 5a7969ae4ea88117a64faac4f42af5c358e213e2
git checkout --detach FETCH_HEAD
cargo build --release
./target/release/semi-persistent doc/book/examples/12-first-au.egg

It prints a single (anti-unify ...) term.

The command-line interpreter reads one S-expression file (.egg by convention). You declare sorts and operators, define two terms with let, optionally add rewrite rules and run them to saturation, and issue antiunify. Two mechanisms tell the engine which syntactic changes do not affect meaning: annotations that assign algebraic properties such as associativity, commutativity, and idempotence to operators, and explicit rewrite rules for everything else. Here is the algebraic part of the signature used in the worked example:

(function Lit (bool) Formula)
(function And (Formula) Formula :assoc-comm-idem :identity (Lit true))
(function Or  (Formula) Formula :assoc-comm-idem :identity (Lit false))
(function Eq  (Account Account) Formula :comm)

And and Or are variadic, associative, commutative, and idempotent, and each has a Boolean neutral element. Eq is commutative. Every reordering, regrouping, and duplication of conjuncts therefore counts as the same term. Nothing else is assumed: Only the stated laws hold, and any further identities must be written as explicit rewrites. The :identity element is what lets the diff align a conjunct that one input has and the other lacks: The missing conjunct is paired with (Lit true) rather than causing the entire And expression to fail to align. Both case studies rely on this identity alignment.

:assoc-comm-idem makes reordered, regrouped, and duplicate operands equivalent. :identity lets the diff align a missing operand with the operator’s neutral element.

Worked example with two policy bugs

The running example ships with the repository as egraph/examples/au_policy_divergence.egg. Consider one policy sentence:

A cross-Region replication request is permitted only if the source bucket has versioning enabled and the destination bucket lies in an approved Region. If the object is tagged confidential, the destination and source accounts must be the same and server-side encryption with a customer managed key must be in effect. Objects up to the multipart threshold are copied directly. Larger objects require a multipart copy.

Two people, or two independent runs of the same model, produced formalizations of it (formulaA and formulaB in the file):

Encoding A (Implies (permit) (And (versioningOn (src)) (approvedRegion (regionOf (dst))) (Implies (taggedConfidential (obj)) (And (Eq (accountOf (dst)) (accountOf (src))) (sseCmk))) (Ite (Lte (sizeOf (obj)) (multipartThreshold)) (directCopy) (multipartCopy))))Encoding B (Implies (permit) (And (Ite (Lt (sizeOf (obj)) (multipartThreshold)) (directCopy) (multipartCopy)) (Implies (taggedConfidential (obj)) (Or (Eq (accountOf (src)) (accountOf (dst))) (sseCmk))) (Or (usEast1 (regionOf (dst))) (euWest1 (regionOf (dst)))) (versioningOn (src))))

Five things differ textually. Three are presentational: The conjuncts are reordered, the Eq arguments are swapped, and approvedRegion is explicitly expanded into two AWS Regions (us-east-1 and eu-west-1). Two involve different operators: An And became an Or in the confidential clause, and Lte became Lt at the size threshold. A unified diff of the two encodings marks 18 of their 28 lines as changed (Figure 1, textual-diff pane) and gives no indication of which of the five differences change meaning. The exact anti-unifier of the two encodings follows:

(anti-unify :size 42 :cr 0.5862 :completion exact
  (Implies
    permit
    (And
      (Implies
        (taggedConfidential obj)
        (And
          (Or (Eq (accountOf dst) (accountOf src)) (Variants (Lit false) sseCmk))
          (Variants sseCmk (Lit true))))
      (Ite
        (Variants
          (Lte (sizeOf obj) multipartThreshold)
          (Lt (sizeOf obj) multipartThreshold))
        directCopy
        multipartCopy)
      (versioningOn src)
      (Variants
        (approvedRegion (regionOf dst))
        (Or (usEast1 (regionOf dst))
            (euWest1 (regionOf dst)))))))

Two of the five differences disappear. The conjunct reordering is absorbed because And is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent (ACI). The swapped Eq arguments have the same printed order in both readings because :comm canonized them. Neither changes meaning, so neither is reported.

**The confidential clause uses Or where the requirement says and.** Encoding A requires both the same-account check and server-side encryption with a customer managed key. Encoding B accepts either. The engine aligns A’s conjunction with B’s disjunction through their neutral elements, so the disagreement surfaces as two adjacent Variants nodes. Choose the first child at each node to reconstruct A: The Or collapses onto the plain equality, and sseCmk remains a mandatory conjunct. Choose the second child at each node to reconstruct B: The mandatory sseCmk weakens to (Lit true) and survives only as an alternative inside the Or. Together, the two Variants nodes show that encoding B accepts server-side encryption alone and therefore admits cross-account replication of confidential objects.

You might have expected sseCmk to be shared rather than repeated. However, a first-order anti-unifier can’t generalize the connective itself, so And versus Or forces the split into two alignments. Identity alignment still shares the five-node equality once. The exact solver’s exhaustive search finds no smaller form, and the printed result is one node smaller than holding both clauses whole in a single Variants.

Add the domain rewrite and run the diff again. The Variants node for the Region is not a bug. It reflects missing domain knowledge: In this deployment, the approved Regions are exactly those two. State that as a rewrite, saturate, and diff again:

(rewrite (approvedRegion r) (Or (usEast1 r) (euWest1 r)))
(run 3)
(antiunify formulaA formulaB :algorithm exact)

The Region difference moves into the shared backbone, and :cr drops from 0.5862 to 0.4000. The full result is the semantic-diff pane of Figure 1. Exactly two disagreements remain: the weakened confidential clause and the threshold. B’s Lt is strict, so an object exactly at multipartThreshold is copied directly under A and takes the multipart path under B. The divergence is confined to the Ite condition. Both branches sit in the shared backbone. Both surviving differences are genuine bugs that an authorization reviewer must resolve. The algebra and one domain rewrite account for the other differences. The same file also runs the anytime search, (antiunify formulaA formulaB :algorithm uct :playouts 3000), which returns the identical size-35 term. The whole program completes in well under 100 ms on an Apple M3 Pro laptop (50–60 ms after the binary is warm). That covers parsing, declarations, saturation, five anti-unification queries with their regression checks, and process startup. We measured the wall-clock time of ./target/release/semi-persistent egraph/examples/au_policy_divergence.egg using a release build at Rust 1.97.1 and the shell’s time command over five warm runs. The Get started section shows the same command.

textual diff: 18 of 28 lines flagged (Implies (permit) (And - (versioningOn (src)) - (approvedRegion (regionOf (dst))) + (Ite + (Lt (sizeOf (obj)) (multipartThreshold)) + (directCopy) + (multipartCopy)) (Implies (taggedConfidential (obj)) - (And - (Eq (accountOf (dst)) (accountOf (src))) + (Or + (Eq (accountOf (src)) (accountOf (dst))) (sseCmk))) - (Ite - (Lte (sizeOf (obj)) (multipartThreshold)) - (directCopy) - (multipartCopy)))) + (Or + (usEast1 (regionOf (dst))) + (euWest1 (regionOf (dst)))) + (versioningOn (src)))) semantic diff: two disagreements, localized (anti-unify :size 35 :cr 0.4000 :completion exact (Implies permit (And (Implies (taggedConfidential obj) (And (Or (Eq (accountOf dst) (accountOf src)) (Variants (Lit false) sseCmk)) (Variants sseCmk (Lit true)))) (Ite (Variants (Lte (sizeOf obj) multipartThreshold) (Lt (sizeOf obj) multipartThreshold)) directCopy multipartCopy) (versioningOn src) (approvedRegion (regionOf dst)))))

Figure 1: The same pair of encodings under diff and anti-unification. On the left, the textual diff flags 18 of 28 lines (removed, added). On the right, one domain rewrite moves the shared structure into the gray backbone, and the highlighted Variants confine the remaining differences to the weakened confidential clause and the strict threshold. The semantic-diff pane wraps one long line to fit

After applying the declared algebra and one domain rewrite, the five textual differences reduce to two semantic disagreements: the weakened confidential clause and the strict size threshold.

Semantic diffing for Cedar and Dogwood policies

In an authorization policy, a dropped guard widens what is permitted and can cause the policy to fail open. Cedar is the open source authorization policy language behind Amazon Verified Permissions. Dogwood extends Cedar authorization policies with temporal conditions for runtime verification of AI agents. Its temporal sublanguage uses recorded event history to guard an action. The engine doesn’t evaluate Dogwood policies. It diffs their abstract syntax modulo a declared algebra. Validation (schema checking) and replay (evaluating a policy against a recorded event history) remain Dogwood’s job. The engine’s user guide has a worked chapter that diffs two independently produced Dogwood candidates for one requirement:

The agent may POST to /deploy, but only if a health check has already come back 200 in the last 15 minutes.

Candidate A keeps both request guards (method and path) but reads the status code from a request event, an event kind that carries no such field. Candidate B uses the correct response event but drops the /deploy path guard. After any matching health check, B also permits a POST to /admin/purge-all. The candidates differ in six additional presentational ways, all of which the declared algebra or a three-rule comparison theory absorbs:

Presentational differenceAbsorbed by
Cedar condition ordereAnd :assoc-comm-idem
temporal conjunction ordertAnd :assoc-comm-idem
predicate field orderargs :assoc-comm-idem
method == "POST" versus "POST" == methodeEq :comm
15m versus 900sunit rewrite + constant fold
count >= 1 versus 1 <= count(birewrite (tLte a b) (tGte b a))

The comparison theory consists of three visible rewrites, not a hidden normalization pass:

(rewrite (mins x) (secsTimes x 60))
(rewrite (secsTimes x y) (secs (IBig::* x y)))
(birewrite (tLte a b) (tGte b a))
(run 4)

The anti-unifier of the two candidates (doc/book/examples/20-dogwood-simple.egg in the repository) has size 61, :cr 0.1864, and exactly two disagreements in an otherwise shared policy backbone:

(anti-unify :size 61 :cr 0.1864 :completion exact
  (rule
    permit
    (head anyPrincipal (actionEq aHttpRequest) anyResource)
    (eAnd
      (eEq (eCtx (fld fInput (fld fMethod fnil))) (eStr vPOST))
      (temporal
        ...
                  (pred
                    aHttpRequest
                    (Variants request response)
                    ...
      (Variants
        (eEq (eCtx (fld fInput (fld fPath fnil))) (eStr vDeploy))
        eTrue))))

Use the simplest available check for each disagreement. Two binary disagreements give four candidate completions. Dogwood validation resolves the first without human review by rejecting both request completions (“predicate … mentions field output.status_code, which is not declared on that event”). The second disagreement is an identity alignment: Candidate A’s path guard pairs against eTrue, showing that candidate B omitted the guard. The requirement resolves it (keep the guard), and a replay covering two decision points shows the consequence: After a health check, candidate B allows the off-target POST, whereas the repaired policy denies it. Combining B’s event kind with A’s guard produces a policy that neither candidate wrote. Choosing between the candidates would have kept one of the two bugs.

Commutativity has a side condition, and the engine doesn’t check it. Cedar’s && short-circuits, so commuting it is sound only when neither operand can raise an error. The comparison therefore relies on validation to rule out order-dependent errors, such as an attribute access that is safe only behind a has guard. The engine doesn’t re-check that condition.

A canonical printer can remove the presentational differences, but it can’t recover a dropped guard. A canonizing printer plus textual diff can absorb most, arguably all, of the six differences in the table more cheaply. No normalizer can align a two-conjunct condition against a three-conjunct one inside an otherwise matched term. Matching modulo the identity element aligns them by pairing the dropped conjunct with eTrue. In a permit condition, that dropped conjunct exposes the widening that makes the policy fail open.

For the Dogwood candidates, the algebra and three rewrites remove six presentational differences. The remaining disagreements expose a schema error and a dropped guard. Combining the correct choices produces a policy that neither candidate supplied.

Comparing policy translations: OpenShell and CEL

The next two examples adapt predicates from the OpenShell and CEL articles. For each, we construct candidate translations of the same requirement. These are illustrative encodings, not recorded LLM samples.

OpenShell: Method and path scope. The OpenShell example models network permissions as predicates over a binary, host, port, layer, method, and path. We adapt the article’s reduced SMT-LIB model, whose path condition is a prefix test. We use that vocabulary for this requirement:

Allow inspected REST requests made by /usr/bin/gh to api.github.com on port 443 when the method is GET and the path begins with /repos/NVIDIA/OpenShell/issues/. Deny all other requests.

Candidate A requires GET and the repository’s issues prefix. Candidate B uses POST and the broader /repos/NVIDIA/ prefix. The other checks appear in a different order. In the encoding, gh, github, and https name the binary, host, and port shown earlier. The names issuePrefix and orgPrefix identify the two prefixes. The exact solver returns:

(anti-unify :size 21 :cr 0.1053 :completion exact
  (And
    (EqText binary gh)
    (EqText host github)
    (EqText layer rest)
    (EqText method (Variants GET POST))
    (EqNumber port https)
    (Prefix (Variants issuePrefix orgPrefix) path)))

The binary, host, port, and layer checks are shared. Their ordering disappears because And is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent. Two Variants nodes identify the conflicting readings: the permitted operation and the path scope. The requirement settles both choices here. For an ambiguous requirement, the same nodes would give its owner two specific alternatives to resolve.

CEL: The scope of a shared condition. The CEL example exposes a production check lost during refactoring. We reuse the expressions as candidate translations of this requirement:

Allow a request exactly when it is in production and its port is either 80 or 443.
// Candidate A
(is_prod && port == 80) || (is_prod && port == 443)

// Candidate B
is_prod && port == 80 || port == 443

CEL’s && binds more tightly than ||, so candidate B applies the production check only to port 80. We encode the expressions with supplied Boolean and integer inputs, using isProd, port80, and port443 for the corresponding input and literals:

(anti-unify :size 13 :cr 0.3636 :completion exact
  (Or
    (And (Eq port port443) (Variants isProd (Lit true)))
    (And isProd (Eq port port80))))

The port-80 branch is shared. In the port-443 branch, (Variants isProd (Lit true)) shows the missing production condition. At is_prod = false and port = 443, A denies the request and B allows it. The diff directs the review to one part of the sentence: whether “in production” applies to both alternatives.

This example assumes that is_prod is supplied as a Boolean and port as an integer. Under these assumptions, neither expression raises an error. The encoding doesn’t model CEL errors or unknown values, and the engine doesn’t check these input assumptions.

CEL-Java’s verification framework can check equivalence and policy invariants with Z3. Such checks can provide evidence when resolving a disagreement. The anti-unifier itself doesn’t decide which translation matches the requirement, and a mistake shared by both candidates would remain shared.

Implementation and performance

The algorithm runs over an e-graph, a data structure that stores a term together with everything it is known to equal. E-graphs (equivalence graphs) come from congruence-closure procedures in theorem provers and were popularized for compiler optimization by equality saturation, as described by Willsey et al. in “egg: Fast and Extensible Equality Saturation” (POPL 2021). This engine’s e-graph adds native canonization for associative and commutative operators.

Anti-unification over e-graphs is also used for abstraction learning and program compression in babble (Cao et al., POPL 2023). Earlier implementations didn’t scale beyond small examples. Our saturation-based prototype also stalled there. Native AC canonization, AC-aware matching over distinct children, and direct search made subsecond queries practical. Semi-persistence reduced the cost of repeated queries.

Native AC canonization. Associativity, commutativity, and idempotence are not rewrite rules in this engine. They are properties of the data structure. Associative-commutative (AC) operators store their children as canonical sorted multisets (ACI operators as canonical sorted sets) at insertion time. One e-node therefore represents all reassociations and permutations of a term and, for idempotent operators, treats duplicate children as one. Equality modulo the declared laws is structural equality. The rewrite-based alternative floods the e-graph with an exponential family of equivalent copies before real work starts.

AC-aware matching over distinct children. Pattern matching against multiset nodes uses maximum-partition semantics: It branches over the distinct children of a node rather than enumerating multiplicity splits, so heavily repeated arguments do not cause a combinatorial blowup.

Direct search instead of rewriting. Anti-unification itself isn’t encoded as rewrite rules either. An exact dynamic programming solver (:algorithm exact) solves the joint-decomposition problem optimally. Optimal here is relative to its size-first objective, the current e-graph, and the configured cycle policy. An anytime Monte Carlo graph search (:algorithm uct, the default) returns its best answer for any playout budget. On the worked example’s pair, 3,000 playouts reproduce the exact optimum. Both optimize first for result size and then, among equal-size answers, prefer those that retain more structure in the shared backbone.

Semi-persistence. The e-graph supports (push) and (pop) snapshots recorded as sparse diffs rather than deep copies. Restoring a state therefore costs work proportional to what changed because the snapshot, plus the cost of repairing derived indexes. Proportional-cost restore lets the engine compare many candidates over one shared graph. A backtracking search can restore an earlier state without copying the full graph.

A verified core and its scope. The e-graph’s underlying container layer is verified in Verus, a verifier for Rust. The verified property is that restore reproduces the state at the matching (push) (1,703 verified conditions, 0 errors). The anti-unification crate proves its objective-order and lower-bound lemmas, but the full solver doesn’t yet have an end-to-end refinement proof.
